Sony Computer Entertainment Japan seems to be intent on making Eye Toy a hit in Japan, where the product has so-far underperformed. Following up on the release of Eye Toy Play and Bandai's Kaiketsu Zororo, the company has now committed one of its most known franchises to an Eye Toy debut: Ape Escape. The resulting title, Saru Eye Toy, seems to add a few twists to the Eye Toy formula.
Like other Eye Toy titles, Saru Eye Toy is crafted from a set of mini games that use the Eye Toy camera to place players in the action. Many of the games involve players shaking their hands in specific positions of the screen for a variety of effects, but others are more involved experiences.
While we're not sure of the number of mini games set to be made available in the game's final version, the version that we tried at the recent Tokyo World Hobby Fair featured dozens. At the show, we spotted a simple game that asks that players shake their hands to free Piposaru (the little ape character from Ape Escape) from ice. Other hand-shaking games see Piposaru run through a hurdle race, bowl and lift a series of progressively growing barbells. One game requires hand shaking to wipe clouds away as players searched for a hidden Piposaru while another has players shake their hands to fix a variety of hairstyles for Piposaru.
One of our favorites, mostly because it just looks so weird, is a mini game that asks players to use their head as a platform so that a bunch of Piposaru characters can run across the screen. At the show, SCE had a guy in a Ratchet costume show this game off.
We didn't get to try them out for ourselves, but a video trailer of the game shown at the event (and available for download in the video section for this story) included some multiplayer mini games designed for up to four players. In one game, two players fight to push over a set of crates to the other side. In another, four players control individual monkeys in a classroom. When the teacher isn't looking, the players have to shake their hands to make their monkey eat a banana. Get caught eating by the teacher, though, and you get shot with a laser!
SCE seems to be making Saru Eye Toy into a Mario Party-style game for the Eye Toy peripheral. While not on display at the show, the final versions' multiplayer mode of play is set up as a board game with players accessing mini-games from the board. Specifics have yet to be revealed, but the board features items that can be used against other players.
Piposaru takes center stage in all the mini games. Like its non Eye Toy sister title Saru Battle, the apes are cell shaded in Saru Eye Toy, giving the game the look of a cartoon, only with your image adding a bit of reality. The bright colors and the imaginative mini games could definitely make this the big hit that Eye Toy needs in Japan.
A Japanese release date for Saru Eye Toy is set for August 5.<|endoftext|>Take a sneak peek at this forthcoming 3DS adventure.
While I've only had a few days with an early version of the game, it's already very apparent that Heroes of Ruin is like nothing else in the 3DS library. A Diablo-stlye action RPG with a huge emphasis on online multiplayer, this new game from Square Enix is bringing quite an ample offering to the 3DS table.
Heroes of Ruin puts you in a world on the brink of ruin - no big surprise there. It's up to you to train up your character and, working either solo or with a group of up to four players, embark on a quest to save the kingdom's ruler (who happens to be a giant sphinx named Ataraxis) from a cursed slumber. The first step is choosing what kind of hero you want to train. There were only a handful of classes available at the time I was playing, including the Vindicators (lions that wield giant swords) and Alchitects (powerful wizards). Naturally, I went with a lion person who I named Mufasa.
The good news is that there are four available player profiles on each cart, meaning you'll be able to go back and restart the game with a different class whenever you want without losing your progress. You're also able to customize your character, though this feature is, at this time, rather limited. For some reason you can only change out skin tone and hair style/color, so hopefully this aspect is fleshed out a little more before the game ships.
While I only barely got my feet wet in the world of Heroes of Ruin, I was absolutely astonished by the amount of content it has to offer. The main quest has you journeying from location to location to solve the mystery of the ailing sphinx king, vanquishing evil along the way. Your character's bread and butter in the defense department is their main attack - which, in the case of my lion, meant swinging his ginormous sword. You can charge your attack by holding down the B button, and you can roll to dodge by pressing the R button.
There's also a robust set of skill trees, which allows you to assign up to three abilities to the A, X and Y buttons for easy use. Do things like quickly dash forward or use a powerful magic attack, the choice is yours, and how you develop these skills informs how your character grows. The game also offers plenty of loot, equipment and items for the taking, so you certainly won't run out of things to collect. A handful of boss fights also help add depth to the experience - and trust me, the main quest is only the tip of the iceberg.
In addition to the main adventure, there are also tons of side quests to complete, as well as a hub town that is positively bustling with NPCs to help and mysteries to unravel. Before too long your Quest Book will start filling up with optional missions you can 
complete along the way - so much so that it's almost daunting to try to complete them all. The game also supports randomly-generated dungeons, which further helps shake things up and makes for some seriously incredible replay value. Basically, you can revisit the same dungeon any number of times and find a different level layout than the time before. There are plenty of secret treasure rooms and the like spread throughout the world, so returning to these areas for fresh loot will certainly be a priority for greedy adventurers.
Of course, one of the game's main draws is its multiplayer. With easy, drop-in/drop-out gameplay, you can share your adventure with up to three other players at a time, either locally or online. To be clear, I only got the chance to test this out with one other player (the servers aren't active yet since the game hasn't been released, after all), but I found that crawling around these dungeons and using the voice chat feature to coordinate attacks with a buddy greatly enhances the experience. If you don't have the inclination to take your game online, you can also complete the whole quest on your own - which is still fun, though admittedly not quite as engaging. Still, with all the content this game comes packing, you won't run out of things to do should you choose to fly solo.
While I've only had a handful of days with an early version of Heroes of Ruin, what I've seen has me excited to delve deeper. I'm not terribly in love with the characters I've seen so far, and I wish you could customize your hero more - but the world itself is strangely intriguing, and the amount of content and scope of the online multiplayer is terribly impressive. All in all, Heroes of Ruin is a fascinating title, one that feels very different than anything else the system currently has to offer. It remains to be seen if all the great parts developer n-Space has put into motion come together into a cohesive, satisfying product - but one thing's for sure, this is certainly a 3DS title to keep your eye on. Will it deliver on all its promises? I suppose we'll all have to wait until its June 26 release to find out.<|endoftext|>"Winky face emoji, heart emoji."

"Freedom of progression." It's a phrase Funcom uses to describe characters creation in The Secret 
World. They've done away with levels and classes, and hope to reshape the landscape of the MMO genre that's been mired in standards for years. But can it break through the confines of familiarity?
The setting, premise, and enemy reveals from The Secret World have been fantastic so far. The work put into the beautiful and dark modern setting of the game is impressive. From the helicopter transport into missions to the abundance of guns and modern clothing, The Secret World is unique and exciting. But it's the character building claims that make me wonder if it'll be able to step away from the definitions of the genre.
Since the early days of RPGs and MMOs, gaining experience, adding new skills, and mastering a particular class have been mainstays. To succeed in particularly tough battles, a cohesive group needed to have all bases covered -- from a heavy offense to a clockwork defense. This was the way of the MMO world.
On paper and in their descriptions, Funcom plans to throw these character ideas out the window. There is no leveling, but by filling an experience bar players gain a skill point rather than a level. This point can be used to gain a new skill, any skill, from the game's wide range of abilities. Forget being a red mage or a monk (too retro of a reference?), The Secret World allows you, in theory, to be whatever you want -- all the time.
This freedom works well when shown off by Funcom in a demonstration. They set up their own character builds and trounced all the enemies in their way. But from everything I've seen so far, I'm still unsure of how players will react to this freedom – after all, players tend to break things and find exploits. Funcom discussed player roles with terms like tanks, aggro, healer, and more common categorizations. While this is a way to place the game's discussion in a familiar genre-language, it makes me wonder if players won't automatically build the same roles over and over again regardless of their options.
This step into the unknown will take some time to balance, but the extensive development time may have given Funcom an edge in finding the new system's equality. It's impossible to predict how the general public will react, but the comfort of tanking, healing, and known ground may be too great to resist in the early days of the game. The power to change is available, but will you use it?
The Secret World's progression is a bold step in character creation and one I'm excited to see come to life. The countless build combinations are all out on the table, so it's up to the player, and not the game, to decide who they're going to be. Are players ready to make that choice for themselves? I foresee my party getting wiped in several encounters because we brought too much fire to the fight, and not enough healing.

Since already dead, the only way to actually kill a zombie is to cause severe trauma to the brain, killing off all brain signals. The way in which the zombies are able to come back has never been fully explained, but they retain some functionality such as the ability to move, attack and react to the presence of sounds.
They are extremely dangerous, often underesimated foes. When alone they can often be dispatched relatively easily, but many a person in The Walking Dead universe has either been injured or killed by becoming complacement with Walkers. They are most dangerous when travelling in packs, where their sheer numbers often overwhelm survivors.
Once a person dies in The Walking Dead, their original spark of life is put out entirely. Their body, or what is left of it, then returns as a Walker.
The time in which the body returns to 'life' is varied. Some people come back as walkers almost instantly, whereas others have been known to take eight hours to fully reanimate.
Once returned, the Walker is devoid of all human traits. They only live to feed, and are able to detect living humans and will do anything to get to the fresh human flesh.
It is believed originally that all Walkers carry a highly contagious virus which can be transmitted either by bite, or in some cases, a scratch.
This is revealed eventually to be untrue - everyone who is alive in The Walking Dead is carrying the virus, meaning that they will always turn into a Walker upon death.
The threat of a bite or scratch from a Walker is still an extremely high threat despite this fact. The bite in particular seems to accelerate the virus' spread throughout a human host, ultimately causing them to lose functionality and, eventually, die.
As a result of this many characters in the universe have taken to drastic actions to stop the spread of the virus, sacrificing others to save their own lives or chopping off affected limbs to hopefully stop the spread of the virus throughout their system.
It is unknown exactly what caused the virus. The series is based not around the discovery of a cure, but generally is focused on characters and the need to survive at all costs.
It appears to only affect humans. Animals that die do not return as Walkers.
In the beginning, the zombie pandemic started out small. It is not know exactly what caused it, but we do know that the rapid spread of the disease was caused by the world being unprepared for such a catastrophe.
In the beginning, the government tried unsucessfully to save the lives of thousands of people by advising they move into cities. This was ultimately the catalyst for the creation of thousands of Walkers; the proximity of so many people together meant the disease was spread extremely rapidly, leading to the cities becoming one of the most dangerous places in The Walking Dead universe.
The infection also spread rapidly through other locations in the universe, meaning practically nowhere is safe.

means the world changes dramatically in The Walking Dead universe. What was once a world of normalcy descends into chaos and terror, leading to those few who have survived doing absolutely anything they can to survive.

Once thrown together, these groups are generally kept intact, with inclusion into the group being an exclusive priveledge for those who are deemed trustworthy. This often leads to deaths in groups, as one member can suddenly turn on the rest and work with other groups, or alternatively leave someone they've lived with for months to die.

Games-as-a-service represents any title that receives post-launch content and consistent updates. In EA's case this includes its lineup of sports games such as Madden and FIFA, which each have Ultimate Team content that entices users to play and spend money year round. EA's MMO Star Wars: The Old Republic and The Sims 4 also have played a role, with the latter boasting six expansion packs and many other add-ons since its 2014 launch.

Point 1 - By combing carefully through the Voxophones, the Luteces must have started their initial experiments with cross-world communication before meeting Comstock. The audio log from Lutece Labs makes it clear that Comstock funded research into the "tears", but since Comstock received his prophecies from a Lutece device, Comstock could not have begun his religion before meeting Lutece since the religion is based around his ability to prophesize. Consequently, the Luteces had already begun creating applications of "tear" theories (or at least the "Lutece Field" theories) before Booker underwent his baptism.
Point 2 - Point 1 implies Comstock used his religion (and lobbying of the United States government) to fund both the development of "tear" technology and the levitation technology used for Colombia. Hence, if there was no Comstock, there would be no levitation or tears.
Point 3 - The "new" Unified timeline at the very end of the game most likely de-tangled the Luteces -- the accident that made them "exist across dimensions" never happened. The implication is that the Luteces knew they would be separated perhaps forever by helping Booker, which adds an extra dose of poignancy to the end.

A group of active and former Infinity Ward members, calling themselves the 'Infinity Ward Employee Group' (IWEG), has filed a lawsuit in the Los Angeles Superior Court today against Activision over alleged claims that the publisher still owes large sums of unpaid royalties and bonuses to the group.
A copy of the lawsuit obtained by IGN states a group of 38 Infinity Ward employees, both past and present, are still owed several large sums of bonus payments as a result of the sales of Modern Warfare 2. Activision allegedly breached its agreement regarding bonuses, and still owes the group between $40 million to $55 million in fourth quarter 2009 payments, between $30 million to $45 million in first quarter 2010 payments, and an additional $5 million to $25 million in other royalties.
The suit also states Activision allegedly has already paid upwards of $28 million in owed bonuses, but purposely and knowingly withheld additional payments to force the team to complete Modern Warfare 3.
"Activision engaged in this inappropriate course of conduct in an attempt to force employees of Infinity Ward to continue to work at a job that many of them did not want just so Activision could force them to complete the development, production and delivery of Modern Warfare 3," the suit alleges.
"In short, Activision withheld the property of the Infinity Ward Employee Group in an attempt to keep the employees hostage so that Activision could reap the benefit of the completion of Modern Warfare 3."
The group is seeking compensatory damages between $75 million to $125 million dollars, and punitive damages between $75 million and $500 million, as well as additional damages.
"Activision believes the action is without merit," the company said in a statement given to IGN. "Activision retains the discretion to determine the amount and the schedule of bonus payments for MW2 and has acted consistent with its rights and the law at all times. We look forward to getting judicial confirmation that our position is right."
Robert Schwartz, the attorney for Infinity Ward founders Jason West and Vince on their separate lawsuit filed against Activision last month, said this new suit invalidates claims made against his clients.
"In 
a lawsuit where Activision is refusing to produce a witness to substantiate its claims, today's new lawsuit by 38 Infinity Ward employees makes clear that Activision's accusations against Jason and Vince are completely false, Schwartz said in a statement given to IGN. "It's great to see the other Infinity Ward people sticking up for themselves. Hopefully Activision will realize that the time has come to live up to its promises."
A full copy of the complaint can be viewed here.<|endoftext|>Big changes could be on the horizon.
The Conan the Barbarian franchise is returning to Marvel Comics in 2019. It's clear that one way Marvel plans on setting this latest incarnation of Conan apart from others is by having the Cimmerian warrior team up with the Avengers. Fans don't have to wait long to see that unlikely team-up, either. Conan will first cross paths with Earth's Mightiest Heroes in March's Avengers: No Road Home #6.
We can only assume this is the start of a larger trend. Marvel may well be working towards establishing the Conan franchise as a regular, influential piece of the Marvel Universe. Here's why we think this crossover could have significant implications.
It's not hard to understand why Marvel would want to create connective tissue between Conan and the Avengers. The prospect of a full-blown crossover is bound to be a huge selling point, one worthy of a major crossover event if Marvel so chooses. We saw some small amount of connectivity between the two franchises in the '80s when Marvel originally held the Conan license, but only on a pretty small scale. This is a chance for Marvel to really explore the possibilities of such an unusual pop culture pairing.
There's also the fact that Marvel needs to do something to establish this new incarnation of the Conan comics as unique and different. Marvel already published hundreds of Conan stories in the '70s and '80s. The franchise has been at Dark Horse for the past 15 years, with creators like Kurt Busiek, Tim Truman and Brian Wood establishing a comprehensive, chronological take on the Conan mythos and earning plenty of critical acclaim in the process. It's not simply enough for Marvel to reboot the franchise and start from scratch. They have to find ways of making this new take stand apart, and establishing a connection between Conan and the Marvel Universe is one way of doing so.
While this first Conan/Avengers crossover is taking place in the weekly limited series Avengers: No Road Home, we can only assume this will be the first of many encounters between Conan and Earth's Mightiest Heroes. The fact that Avengers writer Jason Aaron will also be scripting the monthly Conan the Barbarian comic only lends further credence to that idea. Aaron has long been open about his love for the sword and sorcery genre and Conan in particular. He previously tackled a "Conan meets Marvel" comic in 2015's Weirdworld. We see no reason why he wouldn't take the opportunity to link both his ongoing Marvel books in 2019.
It's interesting to think about how Conan might factor into Aaron's plans for the Avengers. He's already made his mark with that series by introducing the Avengers of 1,000,000 BC, a that includes Odin and prehistoric incarnations of heroes like Phoenix, Black Panther, Ghost Rider and Iron Fist. The current Avengers comic has been exploring a vast cosmic mystery that dates back to humanity's earliest origins. With the series already taking an interest in the distant past of the Marvel Universe, Conan could easily fit into this larger epic. The series could explore the role Conan played (and may still play) in this conflict involving Celestials and gods and superhumans. What if it turns out that Conan himself was a member of another prehistoric Avengers team?
Conan is the focal character in an entire mythology created by writer Robert E. Howard. Known as "The Hyborian Age," these stories take place many thousands of years in the past, after the continent of Atlantis sank into the ocean but before the time of recorded history. Howard's Hyborian Age stories are rich with detail. Alongside Conan himself, they feature all sorts of heroes, villains, gods, monsters, cultures and religions. We could see Marvel hoping to integrate that mythology into the larger fabric of the Marvel Universe. In effect, Conan's world would become a forgotten part of Marvel Universe history.
Not only would this enrich the Marvel Universe, it opens up all sorts of new storytelling possibilities. Could villains like Thoth-Amon still be alive and well in the present day? Might Conan have a distant descendant or two of his own?
We'd also be interested to know if Marvel also acquired the rights to other Howard creations like Solomon Kane or Kull of Atlantis. This could be an opportunity to induct several iconic pulp heroes into the Marvel Universe and forge new connections with Marvel modern heroes.
There are risks to this approach, of course. Unless Disney outright purchases the Conan IP, there's always a chance that the rights will shift to another publisher just as they did when the franchise shifted from Marvel to Dark Horse. Marvel might go through the effort of establishing all these new connections only to no longer be able to acknowledge them. That's essentially what happened when the company made Rom a part of the Marvel Universe in the '80s. Still, there's no point worrying too much about what might happen 10 or 20 years down the road when there are great Conan stories to be told right now.<|endoftext|>How faithful is the new movie to the true Dark Knight?
Batman Begins is not the best comic-book movie ever made, because it is not a comic-book movie. Tim Burton's two efforts, Batman and Batman Returns were dark, moody pieces, but completely unrealistic. After all, it's 
just a comic book, right? Fortunately for fans, Nolan and writer David Goyer saw it differently. The Batman mythos is greater than your standard four-color comic. They say, merely, that he witnessed his parents murder and swore to avenge them by cleaning up Gotham. Batman Begins takes this further. If you want to undertake a quest entitled The Nuka-Cola Challenge, then you're going to have to head to a tiny, tiny settlement in the southwest corner of the Capital Wasteland called Girdershade. Girdershade isn't really a difficult place to find; in fact, if you instantly teleport to Smith Casey's Garage (which you'll have to visit mandatorily in order to access the main quest branch, Tranquility Lane), you can travel southwest from that location and run right into Girdershade. It's underneath a half-destroyed highway bridge, and can't be missed (though it's only made up of a pair of shanties).
Once you're there, you're going to want to head into the home of Sierra Petrovita, which will likely be the house closer to your approach direction. Once inside, speak to the young blond woman within. This is Sierra, and Sierra has the rather strange distinction of being the Capital Wasteland's most ardent Nuka-Cola fan. She has plenty of memorabilia strewn around her home, and is chock-full of both knowledge of and excitement for the Nuka-Cola product. Ultimately, after talking your ear off, she'll offer to give you a tour of her little home-side museum (if you're nice to her, that is).
Agree to take the tour, and then begin to follow her around to all of the corners of the house as she shows you memorabilia and explains to you the history of Nuka-Cola and the corporation behind it leading up to the day when the bombs fell and life was changed forever. Somehow, Nuka-Cola is still available in great quantities in the Capital Wasteland, primarily because of the fact that Nuka-Cola's hub was located in Washington D.C. And just like that, Sierra springs the quest on you. She's really obsessed with Nuka-Cola, but she's really, really obsessed with Nuka-Cola Quantum, a product you've no doubt run into many times on your journey. This blue-hued drink was only in its limited release when the Chinese attack occurred, so it's a rare drink indeed. But she wants you to find some for her. Thirty bottles, to be exact.
Agree to do this for her and she'll give you more information, including the location of the Nuka-Cola bottling plant nearby, where shipping manifests are located. Alternately, you can bring her any Quantum you already have to work your way to the magic number of thirty before you get going. Either way, as soon as you leave her home, you'll be automatically intercepted by an eager man named Ronald Laren, who will initially accuse you of wanting to shack up with his girl (though Sierra isn't even his girl). If you reason with him, you can convince him to take the Quantum from you for the same price, so he can deliver it to his girl and impress her. Especially devious gamers can get twice the amount of Bottle Caps from him as Sierra was offering. Or, you can just kill him. He's irrelevant to the side quest other than offering you a neutral alternative to unload the bottles, possibly for more Bottle Caps.
The Nuka-Cola Plant is located on the far south end of the map. It's due west of the Flooded Metro, and southeast from the Fairfax Ruins and Fort Independence. It's a fairly large building, so it's hard to miss and you should have no issues finding it whatsoever. The enemies you run into, if any, will vary depending on where you are in the game and what enemies you've cleared and not yet cleared. When you arrive at the building, simply enter through the front door.
Once inside, you'll have some options, though your path will more than likely lead in one particular direction before very long. The lobby of the building doesn't have much of interest to you, except for some items to find behind the counter. Along the wall, you can find two Stimpaks in a medical kit. Also behind the desk, in a half-buried metal box, will be a Box of Detergent, some Railway Spikes, and more. The door at the top of the room is extremely difficult to pick open, so we'll assume you can't. To the right, down a corridor, is a kitchen. Plenty of Nuka-Cola can be found within; you'll also have to do battle with one of the building's security robots within. Speaking of Nuka-Cola, you'll find plenty of it here, so don't expect us to mention each and every time you can find it. If you don't find myriad Nuka-Cola here, you're not very good at searching.
Swing leftward down the corridor from the lobby, killing the Protectron you run into in this next computer-filled room. Access the various files on the computers if you want, but there's nothing here you have to read (and as for that safe on the wall, you don't have the key to open it, so ignore it for now). Scour the desks for some various items, although you won't find anything too valuable. 5mm Rounds are about the best you're gonna do here. Then, work your way northward into the next room, killing two more Nuka-branded Protectrons before exploring the various metal boxes on half-destroyed shelves in the room. A Fission Battery and 
a bunch of Wonderglue are the most valuable items you're likely to find here. When you're done scouring, head up the inclining ramp and then go through another door you encounter.
The corridor on the other side of the door is populated by a new enemy called a NukaLurk (which is just a Mirelurk on crack) and a Nuka-Cola Protectron. One will likely fight and kill the other, so you only have to deal with one of them. Follow this linear pathway to the next area of the factory (through the door). You should run into a pair of NukaLurks here --- take them out and begin to explore the room they were surrounding. The most obvious thing is an easily-hacked computer terminal that will awaken a Protectron (hack it for experience, then kill it for even more). Three Pulse Grenades, a Laser Pistol, some Microfusion Cells, a Sensor Module, and plenty of curative items (a Stimpak, a Blood Pack and more) can be found nearby. Then, seek out a staircase heading downward.
This downward-leading staircase will ultimately lead to a Quantum-filled corridor that you're going to be forced to wade through. Just like Nuka-Cola Quantum in bottles, the Quantum flood here is slightly irradiated, but you have no choice but to press through (if you're especially prone to the effects of radiation, consider RadAway and Rad-X your best friends here). Press forward, dealing with any NukaLurks you encounter (there will be at least three). Ahead, you'll see debris blocking your path. Climb a nearby staircase (the second you encounter, ignoring the first one, which is a dud) and then drop down to the path below, on the other side of the debris. This will allow you to reach an otherwise-obscured staircase which will lead to the building's offices.
This section can get confusing, so understand that there's little reason to explore... at least on the first floor. Swing right (heading left leads to a room with nothing), and then swing leftward down the corridor. While you can indiscriminately slaughter weak Radroaches left and right here, you really should focus on finding the staircase leading up to the floor above (a sign that says SHIPPING will lead you along the proper route). Once on the second floor, there's more reason to explore (you can find a Big Book of Science, a Pack of Cigarettes, some 5.56mm Rounds, and a Stimpak, amongst other items), but again, you want to find a staircase leading upwards again. Finally, you'll encounter another door, which will lead you into yet another area of this building's epic interior.
These next rooms are confusingly laid out and connected, so you'll want to explore every crevasse as you progress so you don't get lost. The enemies here are ones you should be used to dealing with by now -- Nuka-Cola Security Protectrons are the primary enemies you'll have to deal with here, though you'll likely be dealing with some other foes as well, from ridiculously-weak Radroaches to horrifyingly-aggressive NukaLurks. You'll also run into a robot named Milo, the still-working mechanical foreman of the facility. You can deal with him in any number of ways, from convincing him you work there to killing him. Either way, search his body (if you kill him), as you're going to need to access the computer in the room he emerges from. No worries for those worried about karma here, either --- killing Milo won't net you negative karma. After all, he's just an annoying robot.
Once you've hacked and accessed the computer in the room Milo was guarding, you'll be able to uncover the shipping manifests, so you can find three great locations to find Nuka-Cola. These locations are ones you've probably already visited, and include the Super-Duper Mart, located near Megaton (you likely already visited this location if you did Moira's Wasteland Survival Guide side quest, easily the longest in the game). Now that you have those goods, however, you should still do just a little bit more exploration before heading on your way. You can find some much-needed Nuka-Cola Quantum in this very building if you just progress a little bit more.
In the adjacent factory room, when you scale the various floors, you should be able to find (amongst a great many items) another computer. This computer, unlike the last one we deal with, doesn't have information on it. Instead, its purpose is to control the conveyor belts below that would send out manufactured Nuka-Cola Quantum to waiting trucks outside. However, the conveyor belt is broken when you try to activate it, but doing so will give you three bottles of Nuka-Cola Quantum to add to your inventory. All you have to do is head down to the conveyor belt and find all three stuck in the machine. Nice!
There's little else to do here. Unfortunately, the locations you're given won't have thirty bottles of Nuka-Cola Quantum within (not even close), so scouring those locations is a good idea, but it won't get you to thirty. This is one of those missions where you're going to have to spend an extended amount of time collecting the goods you need as you do other things. However, you should still go visit Sierra regularly to unload the Quantum you currently have, and to get your caps in return (or, see her stalker for even more Caps). The next generation is coming and you can be damned sure ninjas will be a big part of it. Witness Tiger Hill's first of five videogame related products, ShadowClan, an action-adventure game planned for Xbox 2 and PS3.
Tiger Hill Entertainment is not a developer you've heard of. In fact, it's not a game developer at all. Co-founded by Director John Woo, his producing partner Terence Chang, and industry executive Brad Foxhoven, Tiger Hill is focused on the creation, development, and production of original content for various facets of the entertainment industry. As a content creator that leverages Woo's vision, power, and influence beyond movies, the company's goals are to create killer content, specifically videogames and graphic novels, with the idea of bringing them to film and TV. Tiger Hill has four games in production (one of which is ShadowClan), and is working on creating a feature film based on Nintendo's Metroid.
With sources close to the developer, IGN learned today that ShadowClan is a single-player offline game with a strong online multiplayer component. In the single-player campaign, you take on the role of a skilled ninja with control of multiple AI characters. Pitting ancient ninja arts against modern technology, ShadowClan's gangs comb the landscape of modern day New York fighting rival clans for territory, respect, and power. Your will employ equal parts stealth and action while your gang will be leveraged to deploy strategic attacks throughout the urban levels. Online, the game enables players to build their own ninja clans to confront one another in multiple online maps.

Come over here, big boy.
Our source would not reveal the developer just yet. But we suspect it's an entirely new team comprising industry vets who see this new generation as a great opportunity to create new games. We learned the developer is in current talks with publishers, all of which have shown strong interest in it.
The Xbox 2 and PS3 game is not slated for a fall 2006 release, as was published in Wired. Instead it's being prepared for a spring 2007 release. Expect to hear more on ShadowClan at E3.<|endoftext|>Check out our new obsession.

It's been 15 years, people!<|endoftext|>As the first-ever MAD guest editor.
With "Weird Al" Yankovic taking over tomorrow's issue of MAD Magazine #533 as guest editor, we hopped on the phone with Weird Al and and MAD’s Editor-in-Chief John Ficarra to talk about what to expect.
The pair talked about how this takeover came to be, the difference between written and musical humor, and what Weird Al has in mind for his next project after this (hint: it's musical but it's not another album).
Hear what they had to say, then let us know your thoughts in the comments.
IGN Comics: What's the origin story for you taking over MAD Magazine for an issue as a guest editor?
Weird Al Yankovic: Oh gosh, I've been a fan of MAD Magazine since I was a small child. I've made no secret of that fact. I've been pretty outspoken about my lifelong love and appreciation for MAD.
And I've known John for many years. I believe it was the end of September last year that he took me and my manager Jay Levey out to dinner and pitched me on the idea of my editing this issue.
Weird Al: It literally took me about a nanosecond, I think.
Ficarra: It was something we had been talking about doing for awhile, but we'd seen other magazines do guest editors, and it often felt forced or just cursory in what the celebrity was doing.
So we were always a bit hesitant, but Al had done stuff for us over the years. He did this Jurassic Park special set for us and a couple of book intros, so if ever there was a likely candidate, I think it was and is Al.
Once we said, "Let's give it a go," when we out to dinner that night, it was just a great coming-together.
IGN: So, Al, you're the guest editor. What power does this give you?
Weird Al: "Guest editor" is very generous. I was very involved in the issue, and it's certainly a Weird Al-themed issue, but John and the editorial staff did most of the heavy lifting.
Having said that, I did contribute a few pieces. I was involved in the decision on the cover. I answered all the letters.
Ficarra: You also had all your friends write for the magazine.
I got to pick one of my favorite MAD articles 
from the MAD Vault, and that's featured in the issue.
Even in the articles where I didn't directly contribute, they somehow found a way to wedge me in -- thematically, visually or otherwise.
So this is really a dream come true for me. As a lifelong fan of the magazine, it's still hard for me to wrap my head around this.
IGN: I'll be checking it for typos as well, to make sure you did a good job.
IGN: John, with Al doing all the work, what are you going to do with your time off?
Ficarra: Oh, if only that were true!
We also have several book projects. You know, the way the magazine business works right now, the Weird Al issue is in the art department phase, and I'm already on the next issue. I wish I had more time, I wish. But it was really a labor of love.
It's funny how great it came together. It was a great meshing of the comedy cultures. We've always said that if MAD did music and song parodies, it would be Al who would do them. He's the natural extension of the MAD page, we think.
IGN: What were your words of wisdom for Al when he took the job?
Ficarra: "Stay in music. Don't go into publishing." [Laughs] It pays much better. You get to see the world. I get to see what's out my window, and that's it.
And actually, "Stay out of publishing," because I don't need the competition. He was a very good editor.
IGN: [Laughs] Al, you said you're a lifelong MAD Magazine fan. What's your earliest MAD Magazine memory?
Weird Al: I remember in elementary school, some kids were passing around a Don Martin paperback, so that may have been my first exposure to MAD.
The first issue that I ever read was issue #130, which was the October 1969 issue. One of the guys in my accordion school happened to have that issue and lent it to me. That was pretty much it. That really opened up my eyes, because I had never seen that kind of irreverent humor before. It was a whole different kind of comedy. Something about it really spoke to me.
I became obsessed with MAD Magazine at that point. My parents, my relatives, my friends -- anybody I thought might have some back issues in their attic -- I would con my folks into driving me all over town to used bookstores to see if they had any back issues.
Ficarra: Yeah, MAD is like crack, except there's no rehab.
IGN: John, I'm going to flip it on you. What's you're weirdest Weird Al memory?
Ficarra: I don't know about weirdest, but his recent video "Word Crimes"? If I could make something like that once in my life, I would die a happy man. I think that is the perfect piece of satire. I saw that and clicked on it at work, and watched it. My jaw dropped.
I'd always been a fan of Al's work, but that I think was beyond anything imaginable. I guess because I'm a word person too, I just appreciated the whole subject. It was just perfectly done. Really something.
IGN: What would you guys say is the best approach to written humor, as opposed to something like musical parodies? What's the most important thing to get right when producing content for MAD Magazine?
Weird Al: Well, for one thing, it's a little bit different not having the audio involved, which was something that was drilled into me -- which I already knew, but they made it clear that when you're doing parodies in print, which is something that Frank Jacobs and people like that obviously know, it needs to follow the rhyme scheme perfectly, the syllables need to be in the right place; it has to work very well, and everything has to lock into place exactly so you're able to visualize the melody.
You can take certain liberties when you're doing it as an actual song, but reading a printed set of lyrics, it has to be really dead-on.
Ficarra: "No near-rhymes" is probably the best thing. Al, I don't know what the word is for that, just like the inflection of the word, the way your pronounce the word, whether the emphasis is on the first part of the syllable or the second.
Weird Al: It's more of an exact science when you're doing written lyrics.
IGN: Can you guys tease something that's coming up in this guest issue?
Ficarra: Well, Al is completely throughout the issue, and there's even a surprise he doesn't know about that I'm going to tease him with now that he won't see until he sees the issue.
But from the cover on, we tried to do little Al touches. So you open up the page, and there's an introduction written by Al, and there are some visual background gags that fans of Al will get -- like Alfred from the UHF poster and things. Even Sergio Aragonés, who did the marginals, did special Weird Al marginals.
So there's just lots of nice little touches throughout the entire issue that pay tribute to Al.
Weird Al: That's one of the mind-blowing things about the issue to me, is the people that there were my heroes during my childhood, like Sergio and Al Jaffee, are doing Weird Al pieces in the magazine, which is -- it's just so mind-blowing to me right now.
Ficarra: Oh, and that's one of the great things -- we have Snappy Answers to Stupid Questions at a Weird Al concert.
IGN: Al, obviously you've had great success doing music and now you're doing this stint in MAD. So what's next for you? What dream is unfulfilled for you?
Weird Al: I think most of my dreams are fulfilled already.
This last year has been crazy in the dream fulfillment department. We're about ready to go on a major tour to -- we called it a "world tour" facetiously at first, but it's actually becoming a bonafide world tour. It's 90 percent in North America, but we're also playing the UK and Norway and Denmark and Belgium. I heard we just got offers for Romania and Austria. So it's pretty crazy, but that's the bulk of this year and possibly next year as well.
Beyond that, it's hard to say what I'll be doing. I'd like to continue doing music, whatever movie and TV projects come along. The last couple years I've been floating the idea of possibly being involved in writing a Broadway musical. So there's a lot of options still ahead.
IGN: Last question for you guys, what would 
you say to readers to get them excited to pick up this issue of MAD Magazine?
Ficarro: I think it will be really interesting to see the mashup of the two comedy styles.
I was just telling Al, we have 11 different artists doing caricatures of Al throughout the issue, so that's sort of fun to see the different takes that people have.
And for the first time ever there's going to be an offer for a T-shirt with the cover of Al on it. We've never done something like that before ever, but we just thought that Al had so many fans with the MAD fans mixed in there -- I think if you did a Venn diagram, there'd be a big overlap -- that we wanted to make this as special as possible for everybody.<|endoftext|>Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order is full of new characters in the Star Wars universe, taking place between the prequel movies and the original trilogy - in the "Dark Times" after Order 66 was enacted to wipe out the Jedi.

It is unlocked through the main story quests. Players level 32 and above will be synced to level 31.
The enemies in Haukke Manor will all reflect the dark atmosphere of the instance. Expect to see a lot of undead, bats, and flying eye type enemies throughout the instance. Healers should be prepared for a number of hard hitting enemies, and sleep spells may be recommended to help alleviate the pressure on some pulls. Matriarchs are suggested primary targets as their AOE terror will stun all members in the radius for 10 seconds - stun them or avoid the ring when it presents or it could spell doom for your entire party. It is also possible (and recommended) to pull them solo throughout the dungeon with ranged abilities.
The first boss of Haukke Manor has a strong melee cleave attack which may be lethal to lightly armored players, so let the tank get plenty of threat to start. The Claviger also will cast Void Fire II, a powerful ranged area of effect (AoE) spell, at random. Party members should move out of the radius of the attack whenever it appears. Otherwise, the boss is a relatively simple one that most parties should have no difficulty with.
The Jester and Steward will attack in coordination: the Jester is a spell caster while the Steward is a tank. The Jester uses magical attacks that will do more single target damage than the Steward. The Steward on the other hand has an AOE ability that will drain all group members within its radius. Focusing the Steward allows your damage dealers to stun him before his AOE is launched. In the absence of a party with a stun, focusing the jester and avoiding the aoe is easily done as well. Ensure your party focuses down one target of the two (really doesnt matter which) and this battle will be a cakewalk.
The mistress of Haukke Manor holds the distinction of being the only difficult boss, but a focused group should have no difficulty ending her reign of terror. The Lady herself will use Void Fire and Void Thunder, both of which can be interrupted. Her greatest threat through most of the fight are from four lamps which spawn twice in the battle at each corner of the room.
Until they are right-clicked and deactivated, they will each periodically let out a burst AoE attack against the party that cannot be avoided. They can be healed through for a short time, but extended damage from them will cause a wipe. These lanterns will respawn a second time with "bomb" adds - the bombs will attack your members to stop them from de-activating the lanterns. Bombs are not elites however and the player tasked with shutting down the lamp should easily be able to solo the monster. It is suggested the party determines who will shut down the lamps at the front and back of the room prior to engaging the boss so these can be efficiently destroyed.
When Amandine nears the end of her health, she will become invulnerable and summon a group of adds. These need to be tanked and killed before the boss can be destroyed; a caster-based Limit Break can AoE them down easily, or they can be isolated and destroyed by normal means. I've been to the Tokyo Game Show a few times now, spread out over almost a half-decade. Each time I arrive in Tokyo I'm thrilled by the culture, amazed by the sights, and struck by how different everything is from what we're used to in the States. It's a whole different world here, and one that I hope you get a chance to visit before the world gets too flat.
The Internet is changing everything -- and rapidly. Cultural influence knows no boundaries these days and the economics of making software encourage producers to hit as many markets as possible. Rapid proliferation of ideas and art made easy by computers is making it difficult to stay isolated, quickly encouraging pockets of individuals to join together.
Four or five years ago, a visit to Tokyo would have given even the most seasoned of travelers a bit of a culture shock. The Tokyo Game Show was ground zero. Here was a public game expo filled with what we'd consider niche experiences in the US, heavy on Japanese developer influence, and almost indifferent to the outside world. That flavor hasn't been totally lost, but the beat of change can increasingly be felt.
Back in 2007, the Tokyo Game Show was filled with Japanese cell phone kiosks, Wii and DS games, and lots of scantily clad booth attendants. The girls haven't gone anywhere, but the products they represent certainly have changed.
Go ahead and try to find a Wii game on the show floor this year. A few exist, but they're the exception. PlayStation 3, Xbox 360 and PSP titles dominate the booths, while upstarts in the area have begun to show their faces. For the first time this year, you can find an entire huge section of the convention center solely dedicated to iPhone and iPad games. The number of free-to-play games coming out of China and Korea has grown exponentially, now hitting the point where I've heard people openly gawking at the massive Gamania (a Taiwanese free-to-play developer) booth, wondering aloud how the company got so big. You can almost see where the investment money is going -- and it's not at traditional Japanese game makers.
Still, the Japanese giants that helped to create the videogame industry aren't going anywhere. Capcom, Square Enix and Konami are still major players here, but even they look to Western audiences with 
dollar signs in their eyes. The next Devil May Cry is being made by a European developer as a reboot. Konami is doing the same with its Castlevania series. And Square? They bought Eidos and are pushing games like Deus Ex: Human Revolution and Call of Duty: Black Ops (which it publishes in Japan) at the Tokyo Game Show. Red Dead Redemption is on display at Sony's booth. 'Nuff said.
That quirkiness that comes with Japanese game design hasn't totally been lost. Microsoft -- of all companies -- put a heavy focus on its Xbox 360 support coming out of Japan during this show, offering first looks at several wacky Kinect games. And you don't need to look any farther than GalGun or Asura's Wrath to see that the spirit of insanity is alive and well here.
But for how much longer? With culture intermingling so easily these days, it's hard to say with any conviction that the Tokyo Game Show will remain a unique experience for long. It certainly has changed a lot in just a few years. Globalization appears to be winning. Let's just hope it doesn't sweep through the entire Japanese gaming scene without leaving some room for that special uniqueness it offers.<|endoftext|>Stage 5 returns us to the sewers, but due to a sudden downpour the sewers are full of running water. Revealed as part of the series' milestone year celebration, Sun and Moon look to be both the next step forward for Pokemon as well as a nostalgic look back at where the franchise began.
Over almost 11 months, Nintendo and The Pokemon Company revealed a host of new features, new Pokemon, and new takes on classic aspects of the series. Read on to find out everything you need to know, from every piece of news to every trailer, ahead of Pokemon Sun and Moon's release on November 18.
As part of a Nintendo Direct celebrating the Pokemon franchise’s 20th anniversary, Sun and Moon were officially unveiled via a teaser trailer that kept specifics, and actual footage, to a minimum. Despite little of the actual game being shown, however, IGN did still pick out five cool things in the teaser.
Though shown off later than expected, Pokemon Sun and Moon’s first official footage came in May, introducing the game’s new starter Pokemon — the fire-type Litten, water-type Popplio, and grass-type Rowlet — as well as the brand new Alola region, which, rather than being one big landmass is actually a group of islands. Sun and Moon's Professor Oak-like figure, Professor Kukui, is also introduced in the trailer.
Sun and Moon’s release date was also announced alongside the reveal of the game’s box art, which offered the first look at the new generation’s then-unnamed Legendary Pokemon.
A new month brought a new trailer for Sun and Moon, giving us the names of the Legendaries previously revealed on the box art — Solgaleo on Sun's box and Lunala featured on Moon's art. The new trailer also shed some light Lillie, who is Kukui’s assistant, as well as the player’s friend Hau.
The trailer also indicated that the player's Pokedex would take on new life after it is possessed in the game by Rotom, a Pokemon introduced in Diamond and Pearl.
Sun and Moon was also revealed to have a QR scanner to allow players to register unseen Pokemon to add location markers in their Pokedex to help catch them.
As part of the game’s showcase at E3 2016, Nintendo revealed Sun and Moon’s new multiplayer mode, Battle Royal. The four-player, free-for-all mode determines the winner by the number of Pokemon defeated and the number of party left in a player’s party after a certain period of time.
Another trailer showcasing Zygarde's 10 percent and complete forms also debuted during E3.
After a leak, Nintendo and The Pokemon Company officially announced seven new Pokemon being introduced in Sun and Moon, including Charjabug and Drampa.
Another Pokemon, Salandit, was revealed a week later.
A new trailer revealed another six Alolan Pokemon being introduced in Sun and Moon, including Bewear, Mudsdale, and Mimikyu, which disguises itself as a Pikachu.
In addition to the new Pokemon, Hyper Training was announced, which allows players to improve the stats of level 100 Pokemon. The trailer also revealed that the Pokemon Global Link website will allow players to set up Friendly Competitions and Online Competitions, the equivalent of ranked matchmaking.
An August trailer for Pokemon brought with it a host of revelations about Sun and Moon, including one that harkens back to the franchise’s first generation. Some previous-generation Pokemon will be included in Sun and Moon as new Alola Forms. Ice-type Vulpix, Ninetails, Sandshrew, and Sandslash were revealed, as was a palm tree-like Exeggutor.
The new trailer also unveiled a major story component in the Island Challenge. Trainers are tasked with accomplishing trials on each Alolan island, battling special Totem-form Pokemon as well as the boss trainers of each island, known as Kahunas.
Poke Ride was also introduced, and will allow Pokemon to cross normally impassable terrain in unique situations. Z-Moves were also showcased. These special, once-per-battle moves require the use of the in-game Z-Ring and Z-Crystals so that Pokemon can perform certain theatrical, elemental moves.

All September long, IGN is spotlighting the best TV coming your way in the 2018-2019 season. Today we're taking a look at USA Network's TV spinoff of The Purge franchise, premiering September 4, which brings the horrors of Purge night to the small screen with a new cast of characters who are hoping to survive the night - or create carnage.
With The Purge TV series just one day away - premiering Tuesday, September 4 on USA (with the pilot also being simulcast on Syfy) - IGN can exclusively reveal a harrowing scene from the first episode, "What is America?"
Fiona Dourif plays a crazed cult leader, escorting her flock out into Purge night on a blue-lit bus, where she makes scheduled stops and chooses a... lucky participant.
Does the chosen get to participate in the madness? Oh yes. But maybe not the way you'd think. See, these cultists believe so devoutly in The Purge as a sin cleanser that they offer up themselves as sacrifices to the murderous lunatics out on the streets.
Here, Jessica Garza's Penelope witnesses a co-cultist named Arthur get chosen as the first sacrifice of the evening. And what awaits Arthur outside the bus is - oh - something quite special.
"These cult members come from all walks of life," director Anthony Hemingway (Unsolved, Shameless) told us. "But it's also reflective of one's vulnerability to any larger faction or movement. These are people who fail to have enough self-awareness or strength to see beyond the smoke and mirrors. They're being preyed upon, and it's because they've experienced loss and they have holes and gaps in their lives. And it's caused them to fall into this movement blindly and naively. This particular cult prays on that."
"The thing I love about this series is that we get to delve into stories that the films don't have time to touch on," he added. "We take things a lot deeper, while also remaining a bit ambiguous when it comes to political views or religious views or any of those factions. Though this particular storyline will somewhat shine a light on that area."
One of the most striking elements about this scene, aside from the axe-wielding ponytailed Purgers outside, is the vibrant blinding blue that's used inside the bus. "The 'Purge Blue' is what we call it," Hemingway said. "It the color, when designing the show, that became the palette. When we were deciding on the look and feel for this, we looked at the themes and the characters' stories in the films and blue stood out. It really identified that world. It's what invited you in and it possessed a comfort. A safe feeling. It's also clearly offbeat in a way."
Based on the hit movie franchise from Blumhouse Productions, The Purge revolves around a 12-hour period when all crime, including murder, is legal. Set in an altered America ruled by a totalitarian political party, the series follows several seemingly unrelated characters living in a small city. As the clock winds down, each character is forced to reckon with their past as they discover how far they will go to survive the night. The Purge is written and executive produced by the film franchise creator James DeMonaco and led by Jason Blum.
Hemingway wanted to make it clear that fans of the movie franchise won't be disappointed by the series, and that he and the other creators took pains to make sure the show honored the movies. "Fans aren't going to feel like they're watching something totally different," he said. "It's a cautionary tale. It's what happens if we don't pay attention to our own reality and social climate and figure out how to be an active part in the decision-making process. This series has the ability to really get into social disparity and understanding what that visceral tension and release could be. I think anyone can relate to it."

Approach the blue marker and you will automatically end the level.<|endoftext|>Do you like to choose your own adventure?
Ask a typical RPG fan what he considers the single most vital component of a good role-playing game and chances are he'll tell you it's the story. Probe deeper into that vague answer and you'll likely 
hear slightly more useful phrases like "interesting characters", "meaningful choices" or perhaps "an epic adventure". Which makes it so surprising to see Obsidian take an altogether different approach with Storm of Zehir, the deliberately sandbox-esque expansion for Neverwinter Nights 2.
Make no mistake, this is a marked departure from Mask of the Betrayer, the previous instalment in the series. Where that game was narrow yet deep, Storm of Zehir offers width and expanse. Instead of narrative richness, Storm of Zehir opts for a kind of exploratory freedom that only really works when untethered from the hook of a linear, main quest. If you're expecting a heroic tale where the fate of the world hinges upon your personal sacrifice or redemption, then you'll be very disappointed. If you enjoy testing yourself against wandering encounters, delving into random caverns and dungeons, and just generally finding more cool stuff for your party and levelling up, then Storm of Zehir will hold far greater appeal.
So it works like this: right from the outset you create a party of up to four characters. It's a proper party system, too, rather than a main character and followers. Later you can recruit a further two "cohorts" if you're able to convince any of the more adventurous NPCs to join you.
Immediately it should be obvious that allowing the player to create an entire party inevitably means these characters will lack the interesting backgrounds and personalities that lent so much intrigue to the inter-party dialogue in Mask of the Betrayer, not to mention earlier Obsidian efforts such as KOTOR2. It's a trade-off really: something has to be sacrificed to enable you to design your party exactly how you wish.
The setup arrives quickly, as your party finds itself unwelcome in a foreign land and only able to stay thanks to the protection of a powerful merchant. Adventurers are useful for certain things, you see, and with a helpful leg-up from your new merchant friend you're soon able to establish something of a nascent trading business. And thus a layer of simple economics and resource management is laid on top of the more typical dungeon hacking and looting.
"Why do I always get stood up?"
The world is explored via the Overhead Map, upon which you'll see cities, towns, caves, camps and other places of interest waiting to be discovered. Visit towns and you'll receive quests, many of which involve venturing to a nearby area, killing whatever's there and looting the place. There's also the main merchant quest, but it succeeds more as a guide to the uncharted world and trade mechanics than as an engrossing story.
As a result, most of the time you're just exploring the world via the Overhead Map and checking out whatever you find. You'll encounter bands of creatures, mostly hostile, as well as a few roaming NPCs, such as traders and soldiers. Your party leader's spot and listen skills come in handy here, allowing you to assess potential dangers ahead of time. Further, if you do trigger an encounter, you can use your bluff, intimidate and taunt skills to attempt to give yourself an early advantage.<|endoftext|>IGN: What is the tone of this title going to be? Is it something you're aiming at the core Tex fan base?
Aaron Conners: It was inspired by the old Twilight Zone TV series. Our goal was to create an intriguing, mysterious environment with a story that grabs people immediately and then keeps punching them in the face repeatedly.
Chris Jones: Great twists and turns. Not actual punching.
IGN: While your games have always had a strong narrative and characterization, the Tex games (and Amped 3 for that matter) were all comedies. Is there going to be a humor component here?
Better warm up your brain.
Aaron Conners: Actually, we wouldn't classify Pandora Directive or Overseer as comedies. Killing Moon definitely was, but we felt like Pandora was more in the Indiana Jones vein. Of course, we love humor, but there were serious elements. For this game, our objective was to create an atmosphere of suspense and danger and, frankly, humor can detract from that pretty quickly.
IGN: So what kind of PC are you hoping to target here?
Chris Jones: It won't be a concern. This isn't like Under a Killing Moon was, back in the day.
IGN: Killing Moon was probably the best looking thing on the market in '94. I remember being shocked when I realized the graphics were real time 3D and not pre-rendered. That brings me to my next question: I'm looking at the shots of TCM. Is it safe for me to assume that this time they are indeed pre-rendered?
Aaron Conners: From the beginning, our first priority was to the script, the voice work, the music and sound effects, etc. We initially had a really simple approach to the visuals, but then we decided to up the ante a bit, but the game will not break ground with the presentation of the cinematics.
IGN: What was the initial approach like?
Aaron Conners: It goes back to Tex Murphy Radio Theater, a series of audio plays we did after the demise of the series. Despite not having any visuals (or gameplay, for that matter), we got a great response from the Tex fans. It got us thinking how the voices and music might actually be the most immersive elements -- more than the visuals or puzzles. The initial approach was basically an interactive Radio Theater.
Chris Jones: We do want to stress that Three Cards to Midnight is not like that now. That's how it started out, but it's now a fully visualized game.
IGN: What can you tell us about the pricing and distribution? I know it's not all sewn up yet, but what can you say?
Chris Jones: We're talking to several different parties about distribution deals. We expect to know which way we'll go within the next few weeks. As for the price, it will be under $25.
Aaron Conners: It's a pizza and pitcher of beer! And it'll last longer!
IGN: How long should we expect it to last, and will there be any replay incentives?
Aaron Conners: Six to eight hours. And there is 
definite replayability. The gameplay variables will change when you replay, plus the endgame is determined by how well you played, so people will want to go through it again if they don't get the most desirable ending.
IGN: Why do you think there has been such a stigma with the adventure genre and publishers. I've talked to other developers that have also said even being known for adventure games was a handicap for them. It seems like a fundamentally accessible genre in terms of concept and interface.
Aaron Conners: That's the million dollar question! Personally, we've always preferred adventure games, but, obviously, there have been a lot of stinkers in the genre. Especially during the mid-to-late '90s, everyone and their dog seemed to be putting out adventure games, and that's where full-motion video got its lousy reputation.
I think the staples of adventure games -- namely, things like inventory, logic puzzles, FMV, and especially story -- became associated with tedious, uninspired games. The fact is, there were a bunch of great adventure games and many got overlooked because it was a hassle to wade through the crap to find the gems.
IGN: Yeah, I've heard some say it was the tide of games attempting mimic Myst, a game that worked initially because it was so different, but then became overexposed. Alternately, I've heard the commercial "failure" of Grim Fandango was used by publishing execs to make their case that the genre was over.
Aaron Conners: I definitely agree about what happened to Grim Fandango. That was a great game and didn't deserve to fail--and it was certainly used as evidence that the genre was "dead." That said, we feel that there were common elements of adventure games during that time period that needed to be changed. The audience was evolving and the games weren't evolving with them.
IGN: I know Aaron especially has been a champion of story in games. What is it about games that you think makes them such potent storytelling medium?
Aaron Conners: Chris and I feel strongly that the genre requires a fresh approach. There are things that worked in the past that will still work, but there are other facets that need to be considered. For example, we believe that the storytelling must be razor-sharp and very well paced in order to keep players' attention.
IGN: I know Roger Ebert stirred up some controversy when he said that games dilute narrative, and that story and gameplay are just mixing two different things that don't enhance each other, like chess boxing.
Aaron Conners: Well, I don't totally disagree. Stories are very tricky in an interactive medium. Having written novels and screenplays in addition to game scripts, I would say that the games are by far the most difficult to do well -- which may have something to do with why there are so many poorly done stories in games.
The problem is that the writer doesn't have total control over the story experience. You have to think like a designer and take into account what the players will be thinking and doing. It's also a balancing act between how linear the story is (which makes it easier to pace) and how interactive and free-form it is (in which case you gave the players some control, risk losing the flow and possibly confusing or irritating some players). In a book or movie, the story is told exactly the way you want it, which makes the job much simpler.
I would say that the two can definitely be mixed, but it's a volatile mixture that must be done just right.
IGN: Before I let you go, I'd like to ask what's in store for Big Finish in the long run? Where do you hope to take the company?
Aaron Conners: We're big believers in story-based games. We think there's a market for it and we have lots of stories we want to tell. I would love to have multiple series of games in different genres: sci-fi, historical, children's, etc. I'd like it so people would come to play games at the Big Finish site the same way they go to Barnes and Noble to buy a book. It would also be great to offer aspiring writers and game designer a place to get their start. I've also always wanted to have "guest" story writers and designers who we could collaborate with on games.
IGN: We can't wait to see what you come up with.

You played Shogun 2, right? You didn't? Gah, alright, well like Total War games past, it blended a turn-based campaign map manangement with real-time battles between huge armies. It was a highlight of the venerable franchise, and IGN's favorite PC strategy game of the year.
Fall of the Samurai is set 300 years after the events of Shogun 2. Japan is interacting more and more with foreign powers, which in gameplay terms means you'll get to use Gatling guns and the slow-moving, devastatingly powerful ironclad H.M.S. Warrior to conquer your enemies. You can still charge into land battles with katana and yari samurai, but expect the fighting to be much more Empire-like, with a focus on ranged battles and exchanges of gunpowder weapons.
Japan has evolved in the time spanning the original game and this expansion. There are many who want to see the Shogunate continue, but many others who would rather see the ruling system destroyed to establish the Empire. You choose a side at the beginning of the campaign, selecting one of six clans, three per side. Assuming you know what you're doing and manage to accumulate territory, you'll eventually reach a decision point where you can flip allegiance or stay true to your original cause, which could have a ripple effect across the country, changing the allegiances of other clans.
Not only will you be dealing with other Japanese clans through diplomacy, but can also confer with foreign powers. By making the appropriate upgrades to your port you'll be able to talk with American, French and British agents and even recruit new units to your cause, such as American Marines.
On the campaign map you'll watch Japan modernizes as the turns pass, with telegraph lines and smokestacks rising from the ground. A train line will run down a section of the country as well, and capturing the provinces around it will be important to enable fast transit through your controlled lands. Tracks are only accessible within certain areas – you can't run trains everywhere – so the specific territories become all the more important.
Fall of the Samurai's campaign starts in 1864 and because it doesn't 
span as large a timeframe as Shogun 2, it takes four turns for the seasons to change. This means seasonal conditions will be of much more importance. If caught out in the field during winter, the resulting attrition over the course of one winter could be brutal if you're not paying attention. On the campaign map you'll also be able to take advantage of new agent types.
On the Imperial side the Ishin Shishi can help build support for his side's cause across the map, and the Shinshengumi serves a similar function on the pro-Shogun side. If you decide to hire a Foreign Veteran, you'll benefit from increased experience gain if he's embedded with an army. In cities he can boost army production speed, and on the field of battle he can even call out enemy generals in single combat, which could swing the odds of victory in your favor if you follow up a successful challenge with an attack by your army. Geisha and Shinobi agents will also be available for distraction, assassination and sabotage.
It seems Creative Assembly is also paying a lot of attention to naval combat with this expansion. Numerous new ship types have been added, as well as new weapons like rudimentary torpedoes, but ships sitting offshore can also target cities. You can't direct ships to fire at specific targets like farms of barracks – the cannon fire causes random damage – but the attacks will still help soften up a city for an invasion.
Land armies can also be targets if they're within range, but Creative Assembly doesn't stop there. Ship cannons can actually be activated while within the real-time strategy battles, functioning as Total War's version of air strikes. You need to be particularly careful when calling in mid-battle cannon barrages, though, because targeting is far from precise. You may wind up blasting apart an enemy formation, but could just as easily obliterate your cavalry if you've charged the units too far ahead.
For the Gatling guns or cannon used during land and sea battles, an added third-person control option will let you manually aim and fire. While you gain increased precision for these weapons, you won't be controlling your armies. So while congratulations may be in order for how your cannon fire crumbled the enemy guard tower, you may not be so happy to hear that the rest of your army just got shredded by charging sabre cavalry.
Many more changes, including a redrawn Conquest map for the online portion, updated uniforms and musical themes to reflect the modernized age, and additional historical battles will be included, making it sound as though Fall of the Samurai will be an absolutely enormous expansion. It's a standalone product, which means you don't need Shogun 2 to play. Considering Creative Assembly's track record with Total War and that Shogun 2 was one of the best iterations of the franchise yet, chances are Fall of the Samurai could be one of the year's best strategy games when it's made available on March 23.<|endoftext|>Following a quick use of the immediately apparent Save Point, move leftward until three foes materialize. You too can revel in mediocrity by following him on IGN and on Twitter.<|endoftext|>The Legend of Zelda is a dungeon-crawler. Each dungeon was designed to become progressively harder as you gain stronger items. Some of the dungeons you can complete outside of chronological order, but to gain access to some others requires an item found within a previous dungeon. Each dungeon also was designed to deliberately stump you by keeping hidden key objects needed to progress, such as useful items, Keys, etc. You will need to gather every ounce of courage, wits and patience to best them.
While not all items you pick up throughout your adventure can be put to immediate use, many do exist to serve various functions that aid you in your quest. These items can be accessed in the inventory screen by pressing Start. Highlight the item you would like to use, and it will be assigned to your B button. The A button is permanently assigned to using the Sword (see Items).
All enemies you fight will be enemies that appear in a puff of smoke when you enter the area. The strength and weaknesses of the enemy can vary as you move from one area to another, but generally an enemy of a different color signifies that it is either less or more competent. In this case, red usually indicates the weaker version, whereas blue indicates a stronger variant and would take more hits to down.
If all enemies of an area have been eliminated, they won't respawn after quite some time. Enemies return when Link respawns or after spending some time away. One trick you can exploit is to leave one enemy alive on-screen; doing this deters other foes from respawning and would therefore save you a lot of hassle as you backtrack across the land for various reasons.
As frustrating as it is, when you save, you begin again at the starting location with three hearts (this will be true every time you die, unless it is in a dungeon). You still have all the items you've acquired thus far kept intact in the inventory, but perhaps the biggest annoyance is that enemies you've previously slain will be raised from the dead. Most things, such as doors you've unlocked or walls you've bombed, will be as it were before you saved or died.
To remedy the low health situation that occurs when you respawn, you can visit Fairy fountains located at special points in Hyrule to replenish your health in full. One can be found by heading up from the starting location, then left across a couple screens, past an Old Woman in her cave. On the fourth screen, head up until you arrive in the fountain. Voila! Full health again.
At full, one-hundred percent health Link is able to shoot sword beams that tend to be more powerful than normal sword swipes. If he takes any sort of damage, however, he will no longer have the strength to perform this super move.<|endoftext|>We may not know the complete story behind who Jacob (Mark Pellegrino) is yet but it's safe to say that the person we met in "The Incident" exceeded most rumor and speculation surrounding the character. The second batch adapted King's short story "The Little Sisters of Eluria" and eventually the first novel, The Gunslinger.
