FEC reports also give information about donors, including their address, employer and occupation.<|endoftext|>Just when we thought high-tech medicine had reached its apotheosis in cross-species transplants and the Human Genome Project, we learn that PPL Therapeutics, a British biotechnology company, in conjunction with researchers at Scotland's Roslin Institute, have patented a way of creating clones from the cells of adult animals.
Although the procedure is being portrayed as an advance in science, the profit motive is lurking in the very close background. PPL specializes in the creation of transgenic animals. The company has already implanted human genes into fertilized eggs in order to create sheep and cows that produce milk with human proteins that are then extracted to create drugs. PPL's newest patented procedure will allow animal breeders to produce cloned herds of "meat" animals. The airwaves and newsprint are replete with promises of cloned "low-fat" cows and pigs. The primary purpose behind the technology is clear: to make meat production more profitable.
But concerns about the moral implications for animals has been limited primarily to "animal lovers" or "animal extremists." After all, our conventional wisdom goes, animals are just things, just means to human ends. I suggest that the cloning technology, as well as some of the other miracles of high-tech industroscience, portend a "blurring" of lines between human and non-human. These technologies make possible our creation of moral conflicts, the likes of which we have never considered.
For example, cloning procedures will make possible the creation of "hybrid" organisms that contain specially treated human DNA implanted in animal ova. There will be nothing to stop scientists from creating a work force of slave laborers who are not quite human. And then what? Will we regard these beings as persons 
with rights, or as animals, which are things that we may exploit as long as "we" make a profit?
Cloning is not the only high-tech threat on the horizon. For example, in 1989, Congress initiated the Human Genome Project. Although funding for the project mostly comes from the United States, governments around the world are involved in this research effort intended to map each human gene.
There are legitimate concerns that such a technology will result in a parade of horribles: invasions of privacy, such as the use of genetic information to affect employment, medical or life insurance, or, perhaps, efforts to eliminate certain genes from the human gene pool.
Some hazards have already begun to emerge. Several years ago, the U.S. government asserted that it would pursue patent rights on those portions of the human genome that described how the brain functions. Although the government abandoned this effort, the matter of proprietary interests in the human genome remains unresolved.
But work on the Human Genome Project continues even though there has been little opportunity for public discourse on the effects of such a technology. One clear implication of the project is that it will blur the lines between human and non-human. With complete knowledge of the genome sequence, companies like PPL will acquire an even broader range of profitmaking applications, such as the ability to combine greater genetic knowledge with the cloning process to produce animals with "human" organs. These "animals" could then serve as "organ factories" for xenografts or cross-species transplants.
We mindlessly develop these technologies because we can apply them to animals and then agonize over the morality of such procedures as applied to humans. Most people do not question what scientists do to animals. But the near-term uses of such technologies should force us to confront the reality that there is really no way to draw a qualitative distinction between humans and animals. Seventeenth-Century philosopher Rene Descartes believed that animals were "things" that were indistinguishable from rocks. According to Descartes, animals lacked "souls" and, therefore, could not be conscious or feel pain.
Charles Darwin made it clear that there was no basis for our regarding animals as things. There is no characteristic that humans have--including complex consciousness--that is not shared by many animals. In addition, there is no "defect" that animals have that is not shared by some group of human beings. For example, animals cannot use human language. Neither can some severely impaired people, but we do not conclude that we can use them in experiments without their informed consent or use them to make shoes.
We no longer live in Descartes' 17th Century world. Animals are very much like us.
Dolly, the 7-month-old cloned sheep, is a sentient being with interests. In the debate about cloning and other high-tech industroscience, we have lost sight of those interests.
Bioethicist Arthur Caplan, at the University of Pennsylvania, questioned the morality of human cloning but added that "having identical lamb chops, or duplicate leg of mutton, is interesting, though, if your goal is to eat it." And that is the problem. Perhaps, if we see Dolly, the sheep, as an individual with interests much like ours, we might be better able to puzzle through some of the more complicated issues facing us as a civilization--before our own technologies answer those questions for us.<|endoftext|>Strategies such as shopping for multiple bids on every service and signing multiyear contracts with vendors to avoid rate hikes can help associations save.
The days are shorter, and the nights are cooler. It's the time of year when community association boards and finance committees start working on next year's budget.
Get multiple bids on everything. You'll get better prices, said community association manager Diana Turowski with Lieberman Management Services in Chicago.
"From electric to elevator, architects to tax appeals, knowing that there's competition keeps the vendors honest," she said.
Turowski recently negotiated a 1 percent cost reduction by changing elevator contractors for a client building with a $1.2 million budget. That was $12,000 the residents didn't have to pay.
"Bidding out service contracts can help the board to change to a more competitive vendor or be used as leverage with the current vendor," said Meaghan Bollenberg, community association manager with Lieberman Management Services in Elk Grove Village.
Sign multiyear contracts to lock in pricing. If you've been happy with a vendor in the past, consider an extended contract with an out-clause included, Bollenberg said.
"Vendors may be more willing to reduce future increases for a multiyear contract now," she said.
Start now on next year's capital projects. Going to bid in the fall and winter often results in lower quotes because contractors are looking to fill their spring schedule, said Diane White, senior vice president of condominium management at The Habitat Co. in Chicago.
"Deferring a major project to the future will generally result in a higher price than what it could be completed for today," she said.
White also recommends hiring a project manager to insure the work is completed on time and per specifications.
"Often, such projects are highly time-consuming and complex," she said.
Visit a residential loan officer. Lenders assess the finances of both the association and any prospective buyer. Be proactive, and find out what lenders expect from you, said real estate broker Jane McClelland at Re/Max in the Village in Oak Park.
Lenders have criteria based on how much money is put into reserves each year, the percentage of units that are delinquent on assessments and other financial indicators, she said.
You'll learn how well-run associations manage their finances and the benchmarks to reach for — and you won't jeopardize future sales, she said.
Track your energy usage, even if you have 
a rate contract. If there are spikes in usage on a particular meter that has heavy mechanical equipment hooked to it, that's an indicator something is starting to go downhill, said Ian Novak, vice president and director of condominium management services at Draper and Kramer in Chicago.
"We find tracking utility usage helps identify upcoming problems, so we can budget accordingly," he said.
Ditch the traditional energy providers. Peoples Gas and ComEd are the go-to providers for natural gas and electricity, but associations can save 8 to 15 percent with alternative suppliers, said Gary Kass, president at Kass Management Services in Chicago.
"I reach out to bulk electric suppliers," said community association manager Elizabeth Mosier-Orman at Lieberman in Elk Grove Village. "They can generally provide the communities with a discounted rate for their everyday electric usage in the common areas. This is an easy way to save money for the association, and the brokers have no fee."
Embrace electronic communications. You'll save money on postage, said Jacqueline Abraham, community association manager at Lieberman in Chicago.
"We are sending electronic statements through email for monthly dues instead of sending paper statements through the mail," she said. "We also help associations adopt rules to allow electronic communication and voting to cut down on paper ballots. These measures have saved associations thousands of dollars each year."<|endoftext|>Dear Amy: My girlfriend and I are in our early 20s. We are pursuing our educations. She is a great person. Should I break this off now (before I leave) to ease the pain and explore my options, or should I prolong breaking up until I leave? Am I chasing a love that isn’t really love?
Dear Confused: You seem to be asking about the proper timing for you to break up with your girlfriend. If you don’t want to be with her, then break up with her. There is no “good” time to do that, although sooner is better than later.
Otherwise, I suggest that you leave the timing up to her.
The college years represent periods of massive transition — away from home, into serious relationships, into a first job and out into the world.
It is tempting to try to either delay all of these big transitions (by moving into your childhood bedroom and hiding beneath the covers), or to accelerate these transitions by mapping out these massive life choices and trying to make all of your decisions at once. You have two years to figure this out. Take the time.
The most challenging thing to do is to lean into the uncertainty. You should not pre-emptively make your girlfriend’s choices by deciding to break up with her. Many people relocate to be near a partner, and there are worse reasons to choose a postcollege landing place. The choice should be hers — and hers alone.
What she shouldn’t do is try to emotionally manipulate you into reversing your own plans. If she chooses to move, it will be of her own volition, and she will be responsible for her happiness. If she blames or resents you for a choice she is making, then she is not quite ready for adulthood.

Dear Reluctant: You don’t disclose the timing of your unpleasant encounters with your nephew, but if you essentially gave up on him when he was an obnoxious 8-year-old, then you just haven’t tried hard enough.
Weddings can actually be positive experiences for family members who haven’t been close to reconnect. Of course, weddings can also be estrangement-producing nightmares.
Why express this using such polite and warm language? Because you will feel better if you do. And, yes, because this is your nephew’s wedding, it would be kind of you to send a gift.

Chief Bankruptcy Judge Charles McCormick was reprimanded in a face-to-face meeting Tuesday with Chief Judge Walter Cummings of the 7th Circuit Court of Appeals. At that session, McCormick resigned as chief bankruptcy judge, but will remain as a judge on the court.
Cummings acted on the recommendation of a committee of appeals and District Court judges. Such a censure of a federal judge is rare. It is believed that only a small number of sitting federal judges have been censured this century, while only three, including former Gov. Otto Kerner, have been indicted.
It was previously reported that McCormick allowed one side to write two key rulings without the other side knowing. In a formal letter of censure, Cummings disclosed McCormick has now admitted to following that practice in making two other rulings in the same case and that McCormick has suggested that other federal judges have done the same thing.
Cummings told McCormick that there is ''no plausible explanation'' for his ethical violations. He said McCormick`s ''misconduct here is especially disquieting'' since each of the four rulings favored the side that wrote it.
The action against McCormick comes eight weeks after 
District Court Judge John Grady disqualified both McCormick and a prominent Loop law firm from the $150 million case because of what Grady concluded was collusion in the writing of key rulings.
Those rulings were part of a complex, ongoing case pitting the bankrupt Wisconsin Steel Corp., a South Side company, against its former owner, International Harvester Co. The law firm of Nachman, Munitz & Sweig had been representing Wisconsin Steel, while the firm of Kirkland & Ellis represents Harvester.
In early January, a Kirkland & Ellis attorney realized that the Nachman firm, probably Chicago`s most successful bankruptcy specialists, had received a copy of a major ruling made by McCormick the day before.
But when he called McCormick`s chambers for a copy, he was told the ruling had been mailed only the night before. That meant the Nachman firm had received its copy before the judge`s office supposedly mailed it.
Kirkland & Ellis retained an authority on document examination. He compared rulings signed by the judge with many documents filed by the Nachman firm. He concluded that there were similarities. In particular, two important rulings favoring the Nachman firm were written on paper and a word processor used by the firm.
It is not unusual for a judge to ask both sides to sumbit findings of fact and law when cases are completed. The judge may adopt one side`s version, but the other side has a copy of it.
A judge also may inform both sides of his ruling and ask the winner to draft a formal copy. Again, the other side knows what is going on. In the Harvester dispute, Kirkland & Ellis did not know its opponent was drafting rulings.
Although reprimands of federal judges are rare, Cummings delivered what may have been the last similar rebuke. That was meted out in 1983 to another judge covered by the 7th Circuit, which comprises Illinois, Indiana and Wisconsin. A new Park Ridge law raising the age of tobacco sales in the city is now in effect, just as new bills to do the same statewide surfaced again this week.
Feb. 1 marked the first day of the Park Ridge law, which increases the minimum age to buy tobacco products from 18 to 21. At the same time, possession and use of tobacco, including vaping products, is still allowed for individuals ages 18 to 20.
Park Ridge Police Chief Frank Kaminski said all businesses that are licensed to sell tobacco were notified of the new law’s requirements through letters and in-person meetings prior to Feb. 1.
“They should all be prepared,” he said last week.
Al Shah, owner of Around the World Cigars and Gifts in Park Ridge, said he had been letting his customers know of the impending change prior to Feb. 1, and many of their responses were the same.
“They were telling me they are going to go to Niles or Norridge,” Shah said.
And that’s the problem with the law, he said.
“You’re forcing people between 18 and 20 to go to your neighboring suburbs to purchase the product,” Shah said, explaining that the unequal laws will hurt not only Park Ridge businesses that sell tobacco, but affect sales tax collected by the city and even foot traffic as well.
Shah said he has no objection to an increase in the sale age, but said all communities should have the same law.
Some state legislators are attempting to make that happen. Several downstate news organizations reported this week that bills to revive a so-called “Tobacco 21” law were being reintroduced in the state house.
A previous bill was vetoed by then-Gov. Bruce Rauner in August, and lawmakers failed to override the veto in November.
Kaminski said he believes the minimum age for buying tobacco will eventually increase across all communities.
In Park Ridge, it was the Community Health Commission — a group of appointed citizens who promote ways to encourage healthy living sustainability within the city — that proposed raising the age of tobacco sales in the city after the attempt by state legislators failed. The proposal echoes a national Tobacco 21 campaign, which supports efforts to raise the minimum age for tobacco sales to reduce the number of people who take up smoking as teens and young adults.
Vaping in particular has been an issue in Park Ridge, with a number of high school students ticketed over the last year for possession of electronic smoking devices by a minor.
Kaminski said the police department will conduct its regular tobacco law compliance checks with undercover, underage informants to ensure that businesses are following the new law and not selling to anyone under 21.
Anyone under 21 caught buying tobacco products in the city can be fined $500, according to the city’s ordinance. Businesses that sell to underage buyers also face fines.
Last month, the city of Des Plaines approved an ordinance to raise the age of both sale and possession of tobacco products to 21.

The worst elements of American parochialism and jingoism were bouncing around like Jean Van de Velde's second shot on the 18th hole in the reaction to Van de Velde's play and eventual triple bogey that would cost him a chance to win the tournament.
It was clear that the ABC-TV announcers, Curtis Strange in particular, were rooting against the relatively unknown Frenchman almost throughout the last two rounds.
Once Van de Velde received a favorable ruling that allowed him a questionable free drop during the third round, the announcers pretty much greeted every fortuitous bounce he got as dumb luck while congratulating others, mostly Americans, for improbable kicks on a golf course that is nothing if not unpredictable.
But when Van de Velde, needing but a double-bogey six on No. 18 to win, let eventual winner Paul Lawrie and American Justin Leonard into a playoff with his seven, he was mocked. The references were to clowns played by everyone from Jerry Lewis to Marcel Marceau.
Strange even called him stupid for his play.
This being the same Curtis Strange who in 1985 lost the Masters after going into the back nine of the final round with a four-shot lead.
But instead of laying up on the two par 5s, No. 13 and 15, 
Strange twice went for the green in two, each time hitting his ball into the creek and each time coming away with a bogey. On 13 Strange tried an explosion shot from the edge of the water and the ball rolled back to his feet.
Had he played it safe on both holes, as he was virtually screaming for Van de Velde to do on almost every hole the last two rounds, Strange would have won the Masters.
"It's not in anybody's blood to be laying up there," Strange said then.
Strange, indeed, because Van de Velde did the right thing on No. 18.
He merely committed the great American sin of losing.
Much ignored was the long iron Lawrie hit to the green on No. 18 in the playoff when a layup would have won him the tournament. But Lawrie's shot was true, and he finished with a birdie. And the victory.
In America sporting life is simple: Winners have great hearts. Losers choke.
Perhaps it's why we never bother to learn anyone's language while all the world speaks English. Why complicate things when we already know everything?
Van de Velde made the correct play on No. 18.
He played the 72nd hole as he played the first 71. He played all out. He didn't back off. Sometimes panache can explode and feathers are everywhere.
But it's also one reason why the Europeans do better in the Ryder Cup. They don't play scared as so many Americans do. Take Strange, for instance--he's notorious for his Ryder Cup collapse.
So Van de Velde took out his driver on No. 18, just as he'd done every other time he had the lead. It's who he is. He was predictably wild, but ended on a snippet of land with a good lie.
So he took out his 2-iron. It was the right play. It didn't have the right result.
The trouble on No. 18 is in the rough short and the meandering creek, called a burn. The shot is to carry all that.
Van de Velde carried it. He got the worst break of the tournament, which also went unacknowledged.
He hit the bleachers and his ball kicked back some 50 yards into deep rough. With no bleachers there, he's pin high and chipping on for a par or bogey.
With anything but steep-face bleachers, he's getting a free drop and chipping on to win.
If the ball doesn't hit the stones bordering the burn, he's dropping out of the water, hitting four on and two-putting to win.
But he ended in rough so deep many players barely could advance their ball.
Then he had to get up and down out of a bunker, with all the golfing world's eyes on him, to get into the playoff. And he did, which is a remarkable effort in itself.
That bunker shot and putt were really the pressure shots Van de Velde faced on No. 18, and he was perfect.
The test of a golfer is whether his swing wavers under pressure. Van de Velde's never did.
He played every shot to win the tournament. It's something he should be commended for, even though he lost. But he lost trying to win and never backing away.
When Strange blew that Masters in 1985, he had never won a major. He would go on to win consecutive U.S. Opens, and then as defending U.S. Open champion skip the British Open to play instead for a large appearance fee in another country, great golf traditionalist that he is.
Interestingly, when Strange blew his shot at his first major by hitting into the water when prudence suggested conservatism, Strange was congratulated by the American press for his daring and bravado. The New York Times' Dave Anderson said Strange played "the way he had always been taught a Masters leader should play--aggressively." Sports Illustrated talked about Strange playing at Wake Forest on an Arnold Palmer scholarship and Palmer always preached going down with your boots on.
Yet Van de Velde was knowingly, smugly lampooned.
No wonder people all over the world are always throwing things at us.<|endoftext|>ALBANY N.Y. (Reuters) - Governor Andrew Cuomo said on Monday he had signed legislation making New York the 23rd state to allow medical marijuana, calling his approach, which forbids smoking of the drug and includes strict limits, the "smartest" any state had taken so far.
Under the guidelines, access to the drug will be limited to patients with very serious and terminal illnesses, the drug can only be administered through vaporizing, oils and edibles, and Cuomo reserves the right to disband the program at any time.
"This new law takes an important step toward bringing relief to patients living with extraordinary pain and illness," Cuomo told a news conference at the New York Academy of Medicine, flanked by lawmakers and 9-year-old Amanda Houser, who suffers from seizures.
The legislation "gets us the best that medical marijuana has to offer in the most protected, controlled way possible," the Democratic governor said. "I really believe that this is the smartest approach that any state has taken thus far."
Other states have approved far more permissive laws. Washington state and Colorado decriminalized recreational use of marijuana in 2012. In other states, patients can grow their own pot, obtain it from a dispensary, or both. Medical marijuana is also legal in the District of Columbia.
The signing of the New York law came after years of advocacy by proponents of medical marijuana. While applauding passage of the new law, advocates said it was not as comprehensive as patients had hoped and the timeline was too slow.
"I'm heartened that the governor understands the medicinal benefits of medical cannabis. My son and so many others need this medicine right away," said Missy Miller, whose son Oliver suffered a brain stem injury in utero and now as a teenager has hundreds of seizures a day.
"The eighteen month timeline for implementation suggested in the bill is simply too long for Oliver," Miller said in a statement issued by the Drug Policy Alliance.
State Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver said the state's goal would be to get the program up and running "swiftly, safely and efficiently."
The assembly has been approving versions of the bills for the better part of two decades. The current bill passed both houses 
of the Legislature on June 20.

McDonald’s 74-acre campus — home to the company’s global headquarters, its Hamburger University and a Hyatt hotel — soon will be officially for sale, according to McDonald’s spokeswoman Terri Hickey. Last week, the company put its McDonald’s Plaza property on the market, a 16.5-acre site near the Oakbrook Center mall that could be ripe for redevelopment.
McDonald’s sold one smaller parcel late last year, but still faces the task of finding buyers for the three remaining properties it owns in Oak Brook, which total more than 100 acres.
Oak Brook officials remain optimistic.
“It’s a great opportunity, particularly for a community that’s mostly built out,” said Tony Budzikowski, development services director for Oak Brook.
The first deal closed in October, when McDonald’s sold an office property at 711 Jorie Blvd. to Pennsylvania-based Exeter Property Group for about $14.5 million, according to DuPage County property records. McDonald’s will continue to lease two floors of that building until the move and will retain a smaller office on the third floor after the move, Hickey said.
And across Jorie Boulevard from the McDonald’s campus, the company also owns another 20-acre property on Kensington Road that’s been used by a youth soccer academy in recent years.
Hickey declined to answer questions about that property; Budzikowski said it was his understanding that McDonald’s was selling all of its Oak Brook property.
McDonald’s is represented by Jones Lang LaSalle brokers Scott Miller, Lindsey Fahey and Elizabeth Gagliardi in the Oak Brook property sales.
Oak Brook would like to see another large corporation set up headquarters on the McDonald’s campus, Budzikowski said. Any development involving retail or residential use would require working with the village to change the zoning.
There’s at least one interested bidder already. Inland Real Estate Group is considering redeveloping its current headquarters at Butterfield and Meyers Roads in Oak Brook and making a bid for the McDonald’s campus, said Chairman Daniel Goodwin.
While Goodwin extolled the natural beauty of the wooded campus, which was designed by renowned architect Dirk Lohan in 1978, he said Inland’s preference would be to acquire just a portion, up to 50 percent, of the property.
“My opinion is they may be forced to break it up to sell it. … It would take a very unusual buyer to buy the whole parcel,” Goodwin said.
In addition to the main campus building that comprises more than 330,000 square feet, the campus also includes a 218-room Hyatt Lodge and the 130,000-square-foot Hamburger University, where for years executives and managers have been taught the ins and outs of the Golden Arches.
“At this time we are not parceling off the main campus,” Hickey, the McDonald’s spokeswoman, said in an email.
Amazon qualifies as the sort of unique buyer that could swoop in and gobble up the whole parcel, though competition to land the online retailer’s second headquarters is fierce.
Seattle-based Amazon said it received proposals from 238 cities and regions, but the e-commerce company has yet to comment on which locations are under consideration.
McDonald’s Plaza could represent the more immediate redevelopment opportunity for Oak Brook.
Situated just north of the Reagan Memorial Tollway, the 327,600-square-foot building was built in 1971 and is surrounded by a vast parking lot, save for a Gibsons Bar & Steakhouse on the northwest corner that’s not included in the sale.
The Plaza building could potentially be razed to make room for a mix of retail, residential, hotel and office space, as depicted in a conceptual rendering provided by JLL, although any final plan would be subject to approval by the village of Oak Brook. "Terroir" seems a lofty term in winemaking, perhaps because it comes from the French, but its meaning in English is strictly down-to-earth, trading on the cognate "territory."
For us, "terroir" means the vineyard, its soil and subsoil. When we expand on the notion, we merely conjure a "Truman Show"-ish dome and include the weather (around the soil), the aspect or tilt (of the soil), the life forces (in the soil) and so on.
But we forget — I forgot until a wise winemaker taught me otherwise — a significant aspect of "terroir": the humans who work it, especially over time.
"People influence terroir," says Steve Rogstad, winemaker at Cuvaison in Sonoma's Carneros district in California. "Just as in Burgundy, all that collective experience over a long time — with the vines, the soils, the farming — it's all part of what makes the place," he says.
What follows is talk by other wise winemakers about the human touch on terroir, a story of sorts in steppingstones.
"People generally think of terroir as everything about a site that doesn't have to do with humans. But there's a difference between the land before you've planted it and then after. What humans do to the land always affects the terroir or brings out aspects of the terroir that the terroir can't do on its own."
"Since 1971 I've had the opportunity to plant over 400 acres of vineyards in this special place (the Santa Rita Hills). I've reflected on this. I had been introduced to a beautiful Volnay (a red Burgundy) by a shipmate in the Navy. If I could find the place to make that same texture of velvet in a pinot noir, well. … What jumped out at me was this transverse mountain range near Santa Barbera, where the marine influence was more critical than any other place in California, and there I also found the right soil."
"It's more the 'gestalt.' A vineyard is an artificial construction after all. Vines do not grow in rows and on trellises and produce tiny clusters of pinot noir at 2 1/2 tons an acre. The terroir is a combination of innate characteristics plus all the things about it that can be manipulated and changed. Of course, if you have too much human intervention or too little, you don't get the best from the site. You can 
even destroy it."
"We have 400 acres in vine, on seven distinct soil types, with many different subsoil types, some planted beginning in 1974. So we've had to choose where to plant; location trumps clone. The zinfandel, for instance, goes up in the northern corner where it's warmer, a volcanic outcropping of Mount Veeder, Napa Valley, in Carneros."
"In the vineyard, there is gravel, then sand at 30 centimeters; that is for merlot. Then there is gravel and clay at 80 centimeters; that is for cabernet (sauvignon). We decide what grapes to plant where, but the soil tells us too."
"The best vineyard work is not reactive but proactive, holistic, like health care. That's why we practice biodynamics; it's a closed system that builds up the soils. You want the soils to be healthy so that they can, in a sense, handle a cold; not so you have to 'treat' them for the cold."
"Scientific and technical knowledge is always helpful, but it is in the use of these where problems arise. For example, if you choose your harvest date while you're in the office, you will be way off. In the end, the final decision when to pick is to go into the vineyard and touch and taste the grapes."
The story of humans working the terroirs where their wine grapes grow is a long one.
It is 700 years of Benedictine and Cistercian monks mapping the thousands of vineyards of Burgundy; of more monks forming and planting the vineyards of Bierzo in Spain; of Spaniards and more monks marching up the Mission Trail of California, planting vines as well as crosses.
It is winemakers selecting which clones of grapes to plant where, whether to water, how to prune or trim or splay a plant — all that and more, all human work, human decision, human interaction.
Yep, the hills are alive, all right.
Bill St John has been writing and teaching about wine for more than 40 years.<|endoftext|>Elaine Rodgers Jackson danced at the 1933 Chicago World's Fair, toured with the USO during World War II, sang with a quartet that recorded albums and appeared in television commercials.
In more recent years, that background surprised her co-workers at the Addison Public Library who knew Mrs. Jackson as a sweet and congenial part-time library clerk who returned books to their rightful place on shelves while chatting with patrons.
"Elaine had an amazing life that none of us even knew about, until the day she let drop something like, 'I once did this show with Bob Hope,' and we were like, 'Whaaat?' " said former colleague Karen Dini, assistant department head of adult services at the library. "Then she brought in a photo album filled with pictures of famous people she had worked with — each with a wonderful story. It was really incredible."
Mrs. Jackson, 85, who also performed on WBBM and WGN radio and television frequently during the 1960s, died of natural causes Sunday, March 4, at Elmhurst Memorial Hospital. She was a resident of Lombard.
Born Elaine Rodgers in Chicago, Mrs. Jackson grew up in Franklin Park. At age 7, she performed a Scottish sword dance in the British Pavilion at the Chicago World's Fair.
"It was a complicated dance, but she loved being onstage," said her daughter, Joy Kenyon. "Back then, everyone wanted to be the next Shirley Temple."
After graduating from East Leyden High School in Franklin Park, Mrs. Jackson joined the USO as an entertainer, tap-dancing for troops in the Philippines. Later, she toured the East Coast as a member of a traveling chorus line.
Upon her return home, Mrs. Jackson auditioned with a popular jazz singing quartet, the Meadowlarks, which performed jazz, swing and doo-wop music. She wound up landing more than just the part.
"My father, Maury Jackson, was a member of the quartet," Kenyon said. "Mom walked into the room, started singing and just knocked him out."
The couple married soon after and lived for a while in Chicago before moving to Lombard in 1950.
The quartet recorded several albums under the Chicago-based Chance Records label and performed during the 1950s and '60s on radio and television as well as at such storied venues as the Drake and Ambassador East hotels and the Aragon Ballroom.
During the late 1960s and '70s, Mrs. Jackson sang and voiced television jingles for Budweiser beer, Holsum bread and Capri bath oil. She also appeared in numerous commercials, including one for Ball Park Franks.
"She was dressed up as an old lady," Kenyon said. "After taking a big bite of a hot dog, she jumped up in the air and clicked her heels."
After her husband died in 1986, Mrs. Jackson worked as a clerk at the Plum Memorial Library in Lombard, before joining the staff at the Addison Public Library. She remained there until two years ago, when she retired.
"She was a very sweet lady but also one of the most interesting people I've ever known," Dini said.

Research will tell you, exactly one. The other 19 are dissatisfied with some part of their bodies, most typically their chest, weight, muscle tone and waist.
But it is not all about insecurity that can accompany youth, which is even more pronounced during teen years. A landmark 1997 survey of 548 men published in Psychology Today showed 48 percent of men between the ages of 50 and 59 were dissatisfied with their overall appearance, compared to between 41 and 48 percent for younger age groups.
In contrast, national surveys showed a mere 15 percent of American males were dissatisfied with their body appearance in 1972. That means three times as many men now fret about their looks than when Dr. Harrison G. Pope was beginning his career as a psychiatrist and eating-disorders researcher.
"I see a lot of similarities between men's body preoccupation and how eating disorders among women were considered in the early 1980s," says Pope, a professor at Harvard Medical School and co-author of the new book "The Adonis Complex: The Secret Crisis of Male Body Obsession" (Free Press, $25). "Back then, eating disorders were rarely discussed, then there was an explosion of information. Individual women were relieved to find out they weren't the only ones with an eating disorder."
Fast forward to 2000 and Pope says the "outstanding feature" among all studies about men and body image obsession is the secrecy.
"Almost every one of these men never revealed their problem to any other person, not a spouse, girlfriend, parent, close friend, family member," says Pope. "There's still the taboo that real men aren't supposed to care about how they look."
Pope's co-authors are renowned body image obsession researcher Dr. Katharine A. Phillips of Brown University and Harvard psychologist Roberto Olivardia. Brown has done groundbreaking work on body dysmorphic disorder, a severe preoccupation with an imagined or slight defect in appearance that can prompt sufferers to drop out of school, shun social contacts, not leave home and even attempt suicide. BDD has been diagnosed in boys and girls as young as 6 years old.
The authors developed the term "Adonis complex" to cover the various body image conditions affecting males, including BDD, eating disorders, steroid use and muscle dysmorphia, a newly discovered syndrome in which boys and men believe they aren't muscular enough. The result is they spend inordinate amounts of time in the weight room.
Pope and the others developed a 13-item questionnaire that helps men or their loved ones determine if there are warning signs for an Adonis complex. Some examples: whether they worry (not just think but worry) about some aspect of appearance 30 minutes or more each day, how much time they spend on grooming activities to improve appearance with a half-hour benchmark and if men diet or engage in eating special foods specifically to improve how they look.
"Working out or watching what you eat 
is not pathological, even if you are dedicated to getting to the gym every day," says Pope. "Where someone needs to draw the line is if appearance creates serious stress, when it starts to undermine social activities or school and job status."
Not surprisingly, Pope says American men are in part adjusting self-images for the worse because of the barrage of perfect-body models in magazines and other media--created with more than a little help from black-market anabolic steroids.
More open to debate is Pope's position that the Adonis complex exists in large part due to the continued empowerment of women during the last 30 years.
"Women are in position to become fighter pilots, attend formerly all-male military institutions like the Citadel and move up to CEO of multinational corporations," he says. "The traditional roles of breadwinner and soldier have to be shared. That leaves the body as the only distinguishing factor in many men's minds. The Supreme Court might rule that there can be female cadets, but it can't rule that a woman can bench press 315 pounds."<|endoftext|>America`s Roman Catholic bishops will consider proposals this week to give the nation`s 56 million Catholics fewer holy day obligations for church attendance, and more power to preach on those and all other days they attend. It seems the driver-side air bag-a first for full-size pickups-could accidentally inflate when the passenger door is slammed.
The problem, traced to a faulty sensor, was discovered when an air bag inflated in routine testing. A second air bag inflated when two employees tried to move a truck at Ford's Kansas City Assembly plant.
Dealers have been ordered to quarantine any 1994 F-series pickups until the air bag problem is fixed.
"That means put them in a corner and don't sell them," said James Seavitt, owner of Village Ford in Dearborn.
"I applaud them for that," Seavitt said. "I'd rather not have a recall."
Ford spokeswoman Joy Wolf said 2,000 trucks had been built before the problem was discovered. Though Ford continued to build the trucks, it stopped shipping them to dealers until a supplier could fix the problem.
All of the trucks at factories have been repaired, and dealers will be told how to fix the trucks they've received.
This is the first year a driver-side air bag is available in a full-size pickup. Chrysler's 1994 Dodge Ram pickup, now on sale, also comes with an air bag.
While the problem is causing a delay in shipping trucks to dealers, Ford spokeswoman Della DePietro said there should be no shortage of trucks when they go on sale.
An accidental air bag deployment would be rare, said Wolf.
An air bag inflates when two types of sensors are triggered.
One mounted in the front bumper detects the impact of a crash, the other mounted in the frame of the passenger door indicates when the truck is rapidly slowing down.
When the ignition is turned on, the truck quickly tests the crash sensors to make sure they're working. Ford says that test only takes about 10 milliseconds. But if the passenger door is slammed at the moment of the test, the jolt can trigger the second sensor and inflate the air bag.
That's what two workers at the Kansas City assembly plant did recently when moving a truck off the line.
"Two people got in the vehicle, slammed the doors as the driver turned on the ignition, and the air bag went off," Wolf said.
Slamming doors has not caused air bags to deploy in cars because the sensor that detects rapid deceleration is typically behind the dash board. Ford said its F-series trucks were the first vehicles to put that sensor in a door frame.<|endoftext|>In "Modern-day snake oil needs oversight" (Commentary, July 9), former Food and Drug Administration official Dr. Henry Miller brings up both useful and misleading information.
First 
of all, calling herbal supplements a public health threat is clearly false. An American consumer is statistically hundreds of times safer using herbs than pharmaceutical drugs, which are responsible for more than 100,000 deaths per year and many times more injuries to patients. The side effects of most herbs are minor, by comparison, as herbs are typically more gently balanced than most drugs.
And conventional medicine often treats, rather than cures, chronic ailments, while often causing unpleasant side effects. This drives people to seek alternative treatments.
Still, responsible people cannot argue that these substances require continuing study and clear label cautions where required, especially for their possible interactions with drugs.
I wish that adequate funding for such research were available from the government because there are no patent rights to drive investment in herbal research by drug companies.
Consumers should receive clear guidance on contraindications and maximum potencies on all supplement product labels. This slow process is already beginning to happen, in cooperation with the FDA.
I like Dr. Miller's suggestion for independent certification of purity and potency, and there are GMP (Good Manufacturing Practices) certifications available for companies in the dietary supplement industry. These certifications are relatively new and take many months to schedule and process, so it's still a slowly evolving solution.
Also false is the often-repeated FDA party line that the 1994 Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act (DSHEA), passed almost unanimously by Congress, prevents the FDA from regulating safety, effectiveness or labeling of supplements. The truth is that the FDA was on such a witch hunt against supplements that Congress had no choice but to step in and rein them in. That legislation gave the FDA authority to approve health claims. The FDA already has full enforcement authority to ensure that such claims are scientifically supported and do not mislead consumers. Congress has shown through its enactment of DSHEA that it believes health claims provide consumers with important information.
Unfortunately the FDA is still avoiding its legal responsibilities by routinely denying health claims backed by studies, while not revealing what level of scientific evidence will persuade them. They have even attempted to redefine natural life stages (menopause) to be disease states, in an attempt to prevent label claims for products supporting the structure and functions of a healthy body. The FDA routinely loses these types of actions in federal courts but keeps attempting to overregulate some of the less dangerous substances in the American food and drug supply.
This is not to deny that some herbs are strong as well as effective. There are, sometimes, interactions with drugs and effects on other bodily functions. Let's keep things in perspective by supporting reasonable scientific evidence and rejecting exaggerated warnings, rather than limiting consumer choices while protecting drug companies and overzealous government bureaucracies.<|endoftext|>In the year after an Olympics, the view is two-directional.
One looks back toward the stars of the Games, to see how they are doing after realizing the goals of a lifetime. One looks forward to watch the stars of the future emerge, as they eye the still far-off goal that awaits them three years hence.
The nature of this view changed a little in 1994, when the Winter Games first moved into the midyear between Summer Games, a switch designed to enhance the image of the ice and snow festival. It also changed when enhanced financial opportunities in many sports, both winter and summer, allowed many Olympians to make a longtime job of their athletic career.
So here we are, standing at the end of 1997, on the brink of the next Winter Olympics in February. We gaze distantly toward the final Summer Games of this millennium in 2000 and look back to find emptiness surrounding the 1996 Centennial Olympic Games. They already seem like ancient history because their host city, Atlanta, chose to eradicate nearly all their physical memories.
In 1997, the Centennial Games champion who made the most indelible Olympic memories of the last half-century, Carl Lewis, left the world cheering and his country with one hand clapping as he made a farewell tour. Other gold medalists stepped immediately to the side of the stage: Kerri Strug, the courageous gymnast, was the last Olympian to become America's guest.
Some champions found unexpected challenges in the year after. Michael Johnson overcame a match-race fiasco and a leg injury to win another world track title; swimmer Amy Van Dyken regained enough motivation to return to serious training; swimmer Michelle Smith of Ireland remained in the netherworld between fame and infamy as questions about drug use persisted; rower Steven Redgrave of Great Britain, who had said someone should shoot him if he got near an oar again, couldn't stay away; and swimmer Alexander Popov of Russia recovered from being stabbed in the stomach on a Moscow street.
At the same time, Marion Jones of Los Angeles emerged as track's once and future star; the Kenyan Dane, Wilson Kipketer, showed only being a man caught between two countries deprived him of Olympic glory; a new flock of Chinese women swimmers and runners made a mockery of the year's top 10 performance lists; and the real ancient Olympic host, Athens, became the stage for the first Summer Games of the third millennium.
Those were a few highlights of the first year of the second modern Olympic century. And here, for the 11th straight year, we present our medals to those who made it memorable in the world of Olympic and international sports. As usual, we consider only those for whom an Olympic triumph--medal or other--is the highest achievement.
World Men of the Year: Gold--Wilson Kipketer, Denmark. After missing the 1996 Olympics because he was a few months short of Danish 
citizenship, the 27-year-old native of Kenya rewrote the oldest men's records in track and field. Kipketer broke and rebroke the 8-year-old mark in the indoor 800 meters, then tied once and broke twice the 16-year-old record in the outdoor 800. He was unbeaten, had the five fastest times in the world and an astonishing eight 1997 races faster than 1 minute 43 seconds--a barrier broken only 22 times in history by other men.
Silver--Alexander Popov, Russia. Less than a month after winning his second set of Olympic golds in the 50- and 100-meter freestyles, Popov was stabbed by a watermelon seller in Moscow. The near-fatal blow damaged his kidneys, diaphragm and lungs and allowed him to swim just one race before the August 1997 European championships, where he won a fourth straight title in the 100, a third straight in the 50 and recorded season-leading times in both.
Bronze--Elvis Stojko, Canada. In figure skating's postcompulsory-figures era, when winning more than one world title has become a challenge, Stojko made it three world titles in four years. He also became the first skater to land a combination begun with a quadruple jump and followed by a triple jump.
World Women of the Year: Gold--Marion Jones, United States. From the time she qualified for the 1992 Olympic team as a high schooler, Jones' track and field talent has been evident. Injuries, studies and a second career as a starting basketball guard at North Carolina kept her from concentrating on track until this season, when she won world titles in the 100 and 400 relay and U.S. titles in the 100 and long jump (the first woman to do that in nine years). She had the world-leading time (plus Nos. 3 and 4) in the 100 and the three fastest in the 200.
Silver--Pernilla Wiberg, Sweden. The most multitalented athlete in women's skiing, having won races in all five disciplines, Wiberg last year became the first Swedish woman to take the overall World Cup title. Her nine race victories came in slalom, super-G, combined and downhill--the last a rare skill in Sweden, which lacks the high mountains to produce downhillers.
Bronze--Claudia Poll, Costa Rica. She utterly dominated the short-course swimming season, setting world records and winning world titles in the 200 and 400 freestyles. In long course, Poll was the Pan Pacific Games champion and fastest non-Chinese in those two events.
U.S. Men of the Year: Gold--Chad Carvin. After missing the entire 1996 season with a life-threatening heart ailment, the 23-year-old distance freestyler from Laguna Hills, Calif., returned to win six national titles and five international medals in 1997 and qualify for three events at the 1998 worlds. He finished the year ranked among the world top seven in three events, but a bulging disc in his lower back has forced Carvin to withdraw from the world meet team.
Silver--Allen Johnson. In an event with fierce competition, the 110-meter hurdles, Johnson made it three major titles in three years when he won at the world meet. The 26-year-old Virginian had won the event at the 1996 Olympics and 1995 worlds. He also donated $5,000 toward building a new track at his high school.
Bronze--Maurice Greene. The 23-year-old sprinter from Kansas City ended a U.S. losing streak in the 100 meters--once an event owned by his countrymen--that had included two Olympics and two world championships. He won the 100 at the 1997 worlds, had the world's leading time (9.86 seconds) and four other times of 9.90.
U.S. Women of the Year: Gold--Marion Jones. (see above).
Silver--Tara Lipinski. At 14, Lipinski became the youngest women's figure skating champion in history when she took the title from teammate Michelle Kwan at Lausanne, Switzerland. With her ground-breaking jump combination, a triple loop-triple loop, the New Jersey native who trains in Detroit also beat Kwan for the U.S. and Champions Series titles.
Bronze--Iris Zimmerman. At 16, the fencer from Rush, N.Y., had a season without precedent for a U.S. athlete in this sport. She was the Junior World Cup champion, the world under-17 champion and a foil silver medalist at the world under-20 championship. She also won the U.S. senior title in foil, becoming the youngest national champion in that event.
Men's World Performance of Year: Gold--Sergey Bubka, Ukraine. After already having vaulted into Valhalla, it seemed this track and field god had gone into the twilight of his career. Instead, eight months after Achilles' tendon surgery, the 33-year-old won his sixth straight outdoor world title (14 years after the first) with a meet-record vault.
Silver--Steven Redgrave, Great Britain. On the day Princess Diana was buried, the 35-year-old rower and his somber teammates won the men's coxless four at the world championships. It brought a record-equaling seventh world title for Redgrave, who returned in 1997 to a four-man boat after an 11-year absence during which he won three straight Olympic titles in coxless pairs.
Bronze--Michael Klim, Australia. Previously known for his talent as a freestyler, the 20-year-old native of Poland produced what even he called "a complete surprise" to break the world record in the 100-meter butterfly Oct. 9. He is the first Aussie to hold that world record.
Women's World Performance of Year: Gold--Gianna Angelopoulos, Greece. In the old boys club of the International Olympic Committee, this dynamic, 42-year-old lawyer was a one-woman show in the final presentations by cities bidding for the 2004 Summer Olympics. As bid committee chair, her ability to hold together the factions that had killed Athens' previous attempt was the difference in the city's winning over the IOC voters.
Silver--Cathy Freeman, Australia. In winning the world track title at 400 meters, the 24-year-old became the first Aboriginal world champion in her sport. Calling herself a "proud, indigenous Australian," Freeman expressed both facets of that identity by carrying her national and ethnic flags on the victory lap.
Bronze--Chen 
Yan, China. At the Chinese National Games, the 16-year-old broke the oldest world record in swimming, lowering the 400-meter individual medley mark set by East Germany's Petra Schneider in 1982. When RFK was assassinated in June, 1968, it was an incalculably greater blow to the children in the family than John Kennedy`s assassination had been. Robert had been more intimately involved in their lives, and the children were then five years older.
The eldest, in their early teens, were painfully aware of the depth of their loss. And the Robert Kennedy household, which always had been chaotic, fell apart. When Kennedy was around, he was in control at the family`s home, Hickory Hill. After the assassination, no one really was.
Ethel Kennedy had lived for her husband. When he died, the greatest part of her was lost with him. The focus of her life was to keep him and his memory alive through family ritual and public events.
Although Bobby Shriver does not say so, it is clear that one reason no rules were observed was that Ethel was not enforcing them.
Many people have noted that she kept a strict regimen for herself and tried to get her children to adapt to it (i.e., tennis at 9 a.m., softball at 11 a.m., swimming at 2 p.m., sailing at 4 p.m., etc.), and they simply said no after a while.
She also has a highly developed sense of piety and public image. She wanted her children to go to and perform at memorial masses for their father. She wanted them to participate in the ''right'' summer programs--those that would reflect well on the family and show its commitment to social justice.
The boys couldn`t live up to 
all her demands; so they broke with her.
Bobby Kennedy Jr. tells the story that illustrates the severity of his mother`s relations with those of her children who gave her a hard time. In the summer of 1972, when he was 18, he ran away from home and for four months was never in contact with his mother. When he finally decided to return, he called her at Hyannis Port, Mass., from Nantucket Island and said he was ready to return home. When she gave her consent, he asked her to send him some money because he was penniless and needed cash to ride the ferry.
''Get a job!'' she exclaimed and slammed down the receiver. He ended up panhandling enough money to buy a ticket.
With the girls it was different. She mattered more to them and they to her, and they tried harder with each other.
''She enjoyed her girls very much,'' adds Lorenzo di Bonaventura, a friend of several of the children.
The situation at Hickory Hill disintegrated early in the 1970s to the point where the parents and children in other Kennedy families had to respond. At the Shriver home, where young Bobby was arrested for marijuana use along with his cousin Bobby Kennedy Jr., the parents consciously put distance between their children and Ethel`s.
Ted Kennedy`s children, especially after young Teddy`s cancer operation, were intimidated by the RFK crowd and preferred staying at their own home to traveling the few short blocks to pandemonium central at Hickory Hill.
Jackie`s children had virtually no contact with their RFK cousins for long stretches.
The portrait of Ethel that emerges here is not a pleasant one. Yet it is hard to imagine how it could be. She had 11 children and no spouse, and she had lost her husband in horrible circumstances.
''There wasn`t an hour I spent at Hickory Hill when Ethel didn`t do something to her children that I thought was terrible, or they didn`t do something around her that I thought was worse,'' said a good friend of the family.
The death of Robert Kennedy swept through the rest of the family like a tidal wave. It tortured the children of Edward, who feared they, too, would lose their father to a lunatic gunman. Unlike the older boys in the Robert Kennedy family, who responded by rebelling, Ted`s children, Kara, Teddy Jr. and Patrick, reacted to the second assassination by clinging to their parents. There were also only three of them, compared with 11 in the fatherless RFK home, and it was easier to give them the parental love, time and attention they needed at that period when they were so crucially vulnerable.
Still, of all the families in this generation, Ted`s daughter, Kara, appeared for a while to be in the most danger. Her fears grew, and her life became even more clouded later when young Teddy had to have his leg amputated to prevent the spread of cancer. Then, too, her mother, Joan, sank into alcoholism in the early 1970s.

''Kara helped us all survive--she`s the best,'' proclaims her brother Teddy.
Joan Kennedy`s recovery from alcoholism helped her chart a course uniquely independent of the family, and she has made it a point to instruct her daughter on the importance of being more than a male`s companion.
''Kara has a lot more opportunities open to her than I had when I was her age,'' Joan has said.
''There really aren`t any limits on what she can be. That is a lesson it took me a long time to learn. She has a great head start in realizing that.'' Fortifying an Illinois waterway to prevent invasive carp from using it as a path to Lake Michigan could cost nearly three times as much as federal planners previously thought, according to an updated report.
Scientists warn that if the voracious carp become established in the Great Lakes, they could out-compete native species and harm the region's $7 billion fishing industry.
"Basically during the past year, some additional engineering and design work changed the scope to bring it up to that current cost," Allen Marshall, spokesman for the Corps' district office in Rock Island, Illinois, said Wednesday.

Under the plan, the channel would contain devices including an electric barrier, noisemakers and an air bubble curtain to deter fish from swimming upstream and remove those that don't turn back. The adjacent lock would be retooled to flush away unwanted species floating on the water.

a vice president of the Alliance for the Great Lakes.<|endoftext|>An Audiojack listening session in Los Angeles.
David Tobin took to the stage at a recent technology conference in downtown Los Angeles, asked the 500 attendees to close their eyes, and turned up the sound so they could sample his wares: a textured, layered soundscape that he calls an "audiojack."
A thousand eyes clamped shut as they collectively heard a ball thudding into a glove. A cracking bat. Fans roaring with approval. "How does what you're hearing make you feel? What does it make you remember? There are no right or wrong answers," Tobin told the group, who'd gathered for demonstrations and discussions on how technology can improve the lives of our rapidly aging population. "It's all up to you to imagine," he said.
Taking back our imaginations from an onslaught of words, images, video and other stimuli is Tobin's goal with his business, Audiojack, so named, he says, because he hopes listeners will get "jacked" by the sounds.
A former television producer and one-time manager of the famous Roxy Theater on Hollywood's Sunset Strip, Tobin happened on the idea by accident. After a friend gave him a hard drive that contained a folder of sound effects. Just for fun, Tobin mixed them with no apparent plot or structure, leaving out any human voices. He found that friends who listened to his creation started "putting together a story instantly because your brain associates the sound with memory," he said.
Next he shared it with his mother, a teacher, who brought it into her classroom and saw that kids seemed particularly engaged after a listening session. When a friend sampled it for his mother, who in turn played the soundscape for dementia patients she cared for at a senior center, Tobin began to realize he'd made something that had broad appeal and a useful application.
Senior citizens with even the most advanced memory loss have powerfully responded to his product. One elderly listener who'd not spoken a complete sentence in weeks was able to articulate memories triggered by the sound of cooking breakfast or of a tiger in the wild.
Tobin received similar encouragement from educators and students at the Perkins School for the Blind in Watertown, Mass., who asked him to make more audiojacks, and even invited him in for a group session. Students worked in an on-campus studio to make their own "movie for the mind."
Tobin has not yet conducted formal research into the efficacy of his sound recordings, but researchers in Canada have found that aural stimulation engages older people with memory loss, helping them to be more connected to their surroundings.
More well-understood are the benefits of music therapy, which has been shown in extensive patient studies at Harvard University and Oxford University to achieve reduced stress, and improved mood and social function, as well as regulated heartbeat and breathing. One program, SingFit, offers music playlists with lyric prompts specially designed to engage older people and others with traumatic brain injury.
Audiojack can cite one study by George Mason University that shows improved brain function for people with moderate to severe dementia who used the program over a four-month period. Fernando Roman at the city-funded Echo Park Senior Center just outside downtown Los Angeles has seen this with his work. During the sessions he holds every few weeks, he hands out paper to each attendee, makes sure the room is quiet, and afterward asks them to share what images and feelings the soundscapes have stirred up. Though they're far from the Siberian tundra, much less the woods, the seniors listen and reflect.
"They get to see the wide range of where everyone's mind is at," Roman said. The fact that there are no spoken words makes it accessible to his multi-lingual clientele, too.
Art teacher Michele Mazzei at Edison High School in Fresno, Calif., has seen particular impact with all of her students, but particularly one boy with autism. Typically, he was silent, she said, but when she played one of Tobin's creations, he instantly responded. "He perked up, spoke, and pointed out what he heard," she said. "It got him to be part of something."
Tobin sells the audiojacks for institutional use with lesson plans and prompts, but it's also available to individual users in mobile app form. There's one free available in each category, and an annual subscription costs $14.99. Lately, he said, he's seen a surge in downloads and mail from users who like listening to them for no other reason than to space out. Consider it an active form of meditation, where you can choose to imagine any visuals you like or none at all.
Tobin considers it the antithesis to virtual reality, another popular form of tech-mediated experience. "VR is so stimulating," he said. "You're locked in, your eyes are peeled, you can't get away from it. Here, you close your eyes and do it on your terms."<|endoftext|>This weekend is the annual Retro on Roscoe, when Roscoe Village does the time warp with bell bottoms, classic hot rods and Bozo buckets (see metromix.com for times and details).

Five confirmed cases of whopping cough recently were reported at John Hersey High School in Arlington Heights and four cases at Prospect High School in Mount Prospect, officials with the Cook County Department of Public Health said Thursday.
"It's of concern, because it's a highly contagious infection, but it's not unusual, because we normally see an increase in pertussis cases in the winter months," said Deanna Durica, the public information officer for the county's department of public health, which serves the suburban Chicago region.
In addition, there were three recently confirmed cases of whooping cough at Highcrest Middle School in Wilmette, Durica said.
There were 111 confirmed cases of pertussis, commonly called whooping cough, in suburban Cook County in 2016 through the end of October, Durica said, with a total of 171 cases reported in 2015, and 186 cases in 2014.
According to Durica, every child should receive doses of the pertussis vaccine at 2, 4, 6, and 15 months of age, and then a booster at 4 to 6 years of age.
"It is true that as folks get older, they might need additional vaccines," Durica said. "While there is no vaccine that is 100 percent effective, the kids we've seen with pertussis who were vaccinated seem to get milder symptoms."
At Township High School District 214, spokeswoman Jennifer Delgado said in an email Thursday that officials are "working with the Cook County Department of Public Health on this and follow their guidelines, including notifying parents when a diagnosis is made. We also send parents information on how to look for signs and recommendations to prevent the spread of pertussis."
Delgado said that as a general protocol, the district's maintenance crews "disinfect hard surfaces such as desktops and cafeteria tables, and restrooms every night."
In a Dec. 8 email sent to Hersey parents from the school nurse – one of several emails alerting parents about whooping cough cases at the high school in recent weeks – officials said a Hersey student had been diagnosed with pertussis.
The email included a letter from the Cook County Department of Public Health that said a 12th-grader at Hersey recently was diagnosed with the disease. The letter also laid out steps to prevent the spread of whooping cough.
At Wilmette Public Schools District 39, spokeswoman Holly Goldin said in an email Thursday that the north shore district had three confirmed pertussis 
cases at Highcrest Middle School.
"As the first two were reported, and were in the same team (group of classrooms), parents of that team were notified," Goldin said. "The third case was from a different team in the same grade. At that time, the decision was made to notify the whole grade level. If we learn of new cases, we will notify the appropriate parents."
The district sends parent notifications when it has confirmed cases of the communicable diseases on the Illinois Department of Heath's list, with pertussis one of those listed, Goldin said.
Adults and adolescents usually have milder symptoms than young children, without the characteristic "whoop," but they can still spread the disease to others, according to officials with the department of public health.
While symptoms of pertussis usually appear five to 10 days after exposure and can last as long as 21 days, officials said, with the first symptoms similar to those of a common cold and including a runny nose, sneezing, low-grade fever and a mild, occasional cough.
But the symptoms may progress to severe coughing fits, particularly at night, with "whooping" (primarily in children) and vomiting after coughing, with a cough usually lasting several weeks, officials said.
"Our concern is that since there have been five confirmed cases of pertussis at Hersey, and it's so contagious, we want parents to know if their kids have symptoms of a cough or cold, they should stay home," Durica said. He was worth the wait.
Playing before a near-capacity crowd at HotHouse, Donato buoyantly dispatched several of his hits, as well as lesser-known, but no less beguiling, songs. In effect, he showed listeners why many observers rank him in the same exalted class as the iconic Brazilian songwriter Antonio Carlos Jobim.
Jobim's tunes are more famous, as even many casual listeners are familiar with "The Girl From Ipanema," "Desafinado" and "Dindi."
But Donato's works are built on a similar mixture of high craft and remarkable economy, the songwriter saying a great deal about rhythm, romance and Brazilian culture in a few well-chosen notes.
Seated at the piano and accompanied only by a bassist and drummer, Donato performed his immense songbook with seeming nonchalance, tossing off one exquisite miniature after another. Like most artists who are songwriters first, performers second, he cut to the essence of his music. There were no florid passages on the piano, no pyrotechnics in his straightforward, gravelly voiced singing.
Only songs as elegantly crafted as Donato's could withstand such transparency. Yet each piece Donato played sounded thoroughly inviting, for his music epitomizes everything that is melodically alluring and rhythmically seductive about classic bossa nova.
As soon as Donato announced that he was going to perform "The Frog," a cheer went up in the crowd, for Donato connoisseurs recognized the tune as one of his most famous.
Once again, listeners had to be struck by the deceptive simplicity of this music. Its insistent, repeated-note theme lingers long in memory. Yet underneath this seeming trifle, Donato and his colleagues wove extraordinarily subtle rhythms and cross-rhythms.
Donato's "Amazon" also holds a valued place in Brazilian music, and here, too, the composer layered additional motifs underneath a sleek, attractive melody. After opening the work with a reference to music of Maurice Ravel, Donato slipped seamlessly into "Amazon," enriching it with ultra-sophisticated jazz harmony.Not everything Donato played, however, was quite so melodically lilting. He brought considerable rhythmic tension to his pianism in his "Sugar Cane Breeze"; chanted long, lamenting vocal lines on "Emorio"; and recalled the slightly melancholy style of Erik Satie in a piano solo on Donato's "Aquarius," one of his bigger hits.
Of course, Donato tipped his hat to Jobim, offering an ebullient version of the frothy "I Only Dance the Samba."
Suddenly, the cold chill of Chicago gave way to the balmier breezes of Rio de Janeiro, where Donato now lives.<|endoftext|>Drivers pass by a Redflex red light camera at the intersection of Diversey, Damen, and Clybourn in Chicago on March 1, 2013.

Simpson has left an imprint on the American psyche greater than the sum of his life. Like Marilyn and Elvis and Malcolm, he has achieved in this silk-screening pop culture what passes for immortality.
For those initiated into the small universe of American iconography, their faces are enough. No name is necessary, just the look.
Until the final expression Tuesday of relief and satisfaction, the look for Simpson was the impenetrable public face of the accused, a bronze mask implying neither innocence nor guilt, neither anger nor sorrow.
Through more than nine months of testimony, he left it to the prosecution and his lawyers to fill in what the mask would not reveal. America-indeed, the world of viewers everywhere-could see what it wanted in his celebrity. To some he was a demon; to others, a martyr.
For a young black man raised in one of San Francisco's poor, working-class neighborhoods, the first and second phases of his celebrity-as a college and pro football athlete, and then as a television pitchman-were legend, well deserved, not inherited.
For Simpson it was a remarkable trip from a San Francisco junior college to the Los Angeles Coliseum to the snowy pro football fields of Buffalo, and back to the brittle world of the celebrity rich, the world of appearance, outrageous price tags and a white Ford Bronco in the driveway of his $5 million home in Brentwood, where he returned Tuesday.
Ultimately, the jury in Los Angeles decided it was unwilling to believe his third image, that of a man who murdered his ex-wife and her friend.
"I'm relieved that this part of the incredible nightmare that occurred on June 12, 1994, is over," Simpson said in his first public statement, read by his son, Jason. "My first obligation is to my young children, who will be raised the way Nicole and I had always planned. When things have settled a bit, I will pursue as my primary goal in life the killer or killers that have slaughtered Nicole and Mr. Goldman. They are out there somewhere."
His relief and the jury's verdict notwithstanding, nationwide polls show a majority of Americans believe he did commit the murders. So "The Juice" now becomes a new phenomenon, a celebrity persona non grata, at least to many.
When such a life of glamor and tragedy intersects so dramatically with the public consciousness, it evokes larger themes of race and wealth.
Some saw the trial as holding up a mirror to race relations in America at the end of the 20th Century. There is heavy irony in that, because Simpson's career seemed to transcend race. After the intense civil rights struggles of the 1960s, Simpson became one of football's golden heroes for all Americans.
"Show me a hero," F. Scott Fitzgerald once said, "and I'll write you a tragedy."
Unlike other black professional athletes, such as Muhammad Ali, Simpson had no racial agenda. His close friends were other all-American-style athletes such as Bruce Jenner and Steve Garvey. He played golf. He was just out of college when he won his first six-figure contract as a corporate spokesman for RC Cola.
His fame changed to notoriety last year on a Los Angeles freeway as minicameras in helicopters recorded for 75 minutes a phalanx of police cars following his Bronco, driven by friend Al Cowlings, with Simpson in the back.
In the early days of the murder case, Simpson showed the exhaustion of a person enduring a tremendously emotional experience. But by the time he arrived in court, he had learned the stoic look. He left it to others, including television psychologists, to suggest motivation or defense.
The prosecution tried to convince the jury of what novelist James Lee Burke wrote in "The Lost Get-Back Boogie," that a "human being's life is not shaped so much by what he is or what he pretends to be or even by the compulsions that he tries to root out and burn away; instead it can be just a matter of a wrong turn in an angry moment and a disregard for its consequences."
At the end, he will be remembered most for the accusations against him, the subject of millions of words and 100,000 photographs and tens of thousands of hours of videotape.
Television has been central to his life and his fame, so it seems fitting that the first O.J.-inspired television series, "Murder One," is already a hit after three episodes.
The trial is just the beginning of more books, plays, maybe even opera.
The Orenthal James Simpson narrative begins in the Baby Boom year of 1947 in the Portrero Hill neighborhood, where his mother, Eunice, raised four children in a cramped apartment in a federal housing project while she worked full time as an orderly in the psychiatric ward of San Francisco General Hospital.
She and Simpson's father, Jimmy Lee Simpson, a cook, separated when O.J. was 4 years old. Two years later, a case of rickets left the boy permanently bow-legged and pigeon-toed. As he grew up he sold newspapers on street corners, peddled fish in the projects, unloaded freight cars and worked briefly as a clerk in a department store.
He also got in trouble hanging out with street gangs. He was arrested three times for minor 
offenses, once spending six hours in jail. "I learned one thing," he told an interviewer years later. "I never wanted to go back."
With the encouragement of the baseball Giants' Willie Mays, Simpson left the street life and neighborhood gangs, entering the University of Southern California after a stint at a city college. As a tailback, he took the USC Trojans to two Rose Bowls and won the Heisman Trophy as he was turning 20 years old.
He married Marguerite Whitley, his high school sweetheart, and they had three children, but the marriage ended bitterly a decade later.
By the time he was 25 he was making pro football history by doubling the National Football League record (to 2,003) for yards gained on the ground in one season. In 1973 fans already were writing songs about No. 32, the Buffalo Bills' favorite running back. He would be named Player of the Decade.
Other faces were emerging in addition to that of the athlete. He had begun advertising appearances, running through airports for Hertz Corp. and promoting products from orange juice to Dingo boots and athletic shoes.
He became a spokesman for Chevrolets and sunglasses, for cola drinks and shavers and sporting goods.
Two years before he retired from pro ball he met Nicole Brown, who had just entered a junior college in Southern California. They did not marry until 1985, but long before their wedding she gave up school and her job to be with Simpson.
While he amassed a small fortune, a $1.9 million Laguna Beach summer home and his-and-hers Ferraris, Simpson's face became so familiar that his running-through-the-airport commercial for Hertz remained in people's memories years after it went off the air.
When Simpson was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in Canton, Ohio, in 1985, he wondered aloud whether he belonged with all the others enshrined there. "Well, I must have done something good or something right to be here," he said, "and I just want you to know that I'll never let you guys down."
In the last two decades Simpson moved into Hollywood and other pop culture arenas, becoming a commentator for NBC Sports. He had occasional acting roles, mainly in less-than-memorable films such as "Towering Inferno."
At the same time, his private life was changing. Sydney, his first child with Nicole, was born in 1986 and Justin arrived in 1989.
But over several years, the police were called to Simpson's home eight times because of domestic disturbances.
The year his son was born Simpson pleaded no contest to a charge of abusing his spouse.
